#2836. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#2834. Detroit Tigers Announce Decision on Riley Greene, Spencer Torkelson, 8 Others

The Detroit Tigers have made their decisions ahead of Major League Baseball's non-tender deadline, and several familiar faces will remain under team control heading into the 2027 season.

That includes two of Detroit's biggest offensive names.

On Friday, the Tigers announced that they have tendered 2027 contracts to Riley Greene, Spencer Torkelson, and eight additional arbitration-eligible players, ending speculation about whether some members of the roster could become free agents.

The announcement also confirms the departure of three players who were designated for assignment earlier this week.

For president of baseball operations Scott Harris, the decisions provide some clarity as Detroit continues reshaping its roster for next season.

And for Torkelson in particular, Friday's announcement answers a question that had been generating considerable discussion.

According to the Tigers' official public relations account, Detroit tendered 2027 contracts to the following arbitration-eligible players:

The decision means Detroit has retained the contractual rights to all 10 players rather than allowing them to enter free agency through the non-tender process.

However, tendering a contract does not mean the Tigers have agreed to new salaries with each player.

Those figures will be negotiated through MLB's arbitration process, with hearings possible if the two sides cannot reach agreements.

The Tigers also announced that all 21 players on their 40-man roster who are not yet arbitration-eligible have received contract tenders for 2027.

While the decisions involving Greene, Carpenter, and several other players were widely expected, Torkelson and McKinstry had attracted additional attention ahead of Friday's deadline.

Torkelson's future was particularly interesting because the former No. 1 overall draft pick is projected to earn a substantial raise through arbitration.

As previously discussed ahead of the deadline, Detroit faced a decision about whether keeping Torkelson at his projected salary made sense after another uneven season.

The Tigers ultimately decided to retain his rights rather than create an immediate opening at first base.

McKinstry was another potential non-tender candidate after struggling offensively during the 2026 campaign.

Detroit had been facing a significant decision regarding McKinstry's future, but Friday's announcement confirms he remains under team control.

Of course, neither decision guarantees those players will be on Detroit's Opening Day roster.

The Tigers can still explore trades or make additional roster changes during the offseason.

While Detroit retained its 10 arbitration-eligible players, the organization also confirmed that three others have been formally non-tendered.

All three had previously been designated for assignment on Tuesday, November 17, as Detroit made room for additional players on its 40-man roster.

Friday's decision brings their time on Detroit's current roster to an end, with the players now free to explore opportunities elsewhere.

The Tigers had already made several roster moves ahead of the Rule 5 protection deadline, and the latest announcement completes another important step in their offseason planning.

Detroit also confirmed that its 40-man roster remains full at 40 players, meaning additional moves would be necessary to create space for any new players requiring a roster spot.

Friday's announcement doesn't necessarily contain a major surprise, but it does provide some important answers about Detroit's immediate plans.

Greene and Carpenter remain part of the team's outfield picture, while Torkelson will continue to be an option at first base. The Tigers also retained several important pitching pieces, including Olson, Vest, Holton, and Brieske.

And with Detroit having already reportedly agreed to a six-year, $46.5 million extension with Troy Melton earlier Friday, Harris is beginning to provide some direction for the organization's pitching future.

Tendering contracts keeps these players under team control, but it doesn't prevent the Tigers from making trades or pursuing upgrades before Opening Day.

For now, though, two of the biggest questions surrounding Detroit's arbitration-eligible roster have been answered.

Riley Greene and Spencer Torkelson aren't becoming free agents through the non-tender process.

Whether both remain Tigers when the 2027 season begins is another question entirely.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2832. Jimmy Garoppolo’s reunion may not be with the Rams

If the Los Angeles Rams lost Matthew Stafford for any amount of time this season, would you trust the current backup quarterback options?

Would you feel any better if an experienced veteran, like Jimmy Garoppolo, could step in?

There's nothing to indicate Stafford is at any increased risk of an injury or missing snaps for any reason. But as the NFL playoffs approach and the margin for error shrinks closer to zero, it's hard not to think about protecting yourself against calamity. That's especially true for a Rams team that has dealt with tons of injuries this year, including another serious one to a starting offensive lineman just this week.

This is relevant now because Garoppolo, who spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons in Los Angeles, is suddenly being linked to other playoff contenders, like another one of his former teams, the New England Patriots.

After initial reporting on the matter by Jordan Schultz, ESPN's Jeremy Fowler discussed the situation this week and threw some cold water on the topic but stopped short of completely killing the idea. Specifically, he mentioned that there are questions about whether or not the 12-year veteran has any actual desire to play again.

He also mentioned, however, that Garoppolo enjoyed playing on the west coast. That could work in the Rams' favor, obviously.

Don't get it twisted, this is not an earth-shattering kind of hypothetical personnel scenario. This is a quarterback who had good moments in several years as a starter, but isn't exactly a Hall of Fame candidate. He would purely be an insurance policy if Los Angeles wanted to pursue that route. And realistically, if Stafford missed more than a game or a couple games at the absolute most, things would get dire in a hurry for the Rams.

Still, the alternatives currently are Stetson Bennett, who's taken a whopping 10 offensive snaps over four seasons (all of which have come this year) and Ty Simpson, the first-round pick who still hasn't seen the field and who is a known project player.

This idea isn't completely out of left field, either, as it was discussed over the offseason as the backup job was still in flux in the wake of the Simpson pick in the NFL draft. There isn't much that's controversial about re-signing a generally inoffensive backup quarterback.

The Rams have enough personnel concerns that they likely don't have to go full bore after another reserve quarterback right now. But if push came to shove and they had to sign one out of desperation, Garoppolo still makes sense. That's the situation the Patriots are quite literally in right now with Drake Maye injured.

It would be a terrible scenario regardless, but a slightly less devastating one with a more reliable backup in the fray.

#2830. Ranking all the scary comments Steph Curry makes in the ESPN article

Three days ago, ESPN's Anthony Slater published a story that served to remind us all that time slows for no one and that Steph Curry's playing days are numbered. It was startling. The specifics of it were so definitive, so obviously instructive of how the music would suddenly stop, that many fans were (rightfully) shook. Every quote feels like a night night dagger; but, since this is a sports blog, let's rank them by order of "BANG!"-itude.

First: if you haven't read the piece, go and read it, because I'll be jumping around.

Is this actually a scary quote? Not totally. We must always remember that a professional athlete who has played at the highest level possible for a human being during this moment in time lives in the moment most of the time. But you know the end is on the horizon once the athlete begins to discuss the end. Most of our stars have been stuck in some version of that kid who loved the game they played and wound up making millions for doing and mere recognition of mortality is revolutionary in terms of self-reflection. But the scare factor is that Steph's aware the party's winding down. His body has been telling him, and now his conscious thought has joined the fray.

This is a heightening of that recognition. A recognition of context, but also "the ability to convince myself" is a heckuva self-reflection. His mind is asking his body to prove it, and — for now — it's satisfying his standards. Will he lower his standards to keep convincing himself? Or does he have a "If I can't do 'x' anymore, then that's it" in mind?

Slater gets quotes from Steve Kerr in this piece, too, and for this segment he relates:

"He's staying off his feet [more often]," Kerr said. "Relying on the fact that he's built up this incredible skill level that's not going to leave him. Then, he's found a way to stay really fit without pounding the knees, the ankles. He's on the bike, underwater treadmill. He's creative."

But I'm putting this 8th because I'm a little scared by how this aging curve seems to have surprised Curry. Slater begins the article by talking about earlier this year, and that being the first time he really seemed to have grappled with his aging body.

Every athlete — every human being! — is different, of course, so this isn't a criticism, it's just a note that Steph Curry is not one of those athletes who plans too far ahead. His greatness has been defined by putting the pedal to the metal at all times; but, everyone in their mid-thirties would be wise to reassess their body maintenance. You can see how the idea of leaving something on the table doesn't appeal to him. It's not a lack of wisdom or intelligence, it's just the way that he is wired. But as a fan reading this, the fear factor is in how he's just going to keep dancing until the music stops.

Well, okay, and then there's an acknowledgement that he needs to slow some aspect of it down. This line definitely amps up the bummer vibes of the piece. It's like he's counting how many sunrises he's got left.

Or counting how many more sandwiches he'll have left to eat in his life. But you can see why Dylan Thomas urged rage because contemplation or otherwise quiet reflection is just a bummer. It sucks to be reminded that this is all going to end — better to burn out than fade away, right? But that's the tension of being a professional athlete. That's certainly the trajectory Steph is on; will this slowdown prolong his career?

This is the first quote of the aptly titled article, "The clock is ticking on Steph Curry's final act with the Warriors." Slater starts with an anecdote about an off-day workout going awry and quickly pulls in the oblique abdominal strain, but the constant throughout the article is Steph's knee.

"a weird soreness and pain that didn't go away"

"It was basically holding. It wasn't going either direction."

There's even discussion of how much it held him back, where he was just going through the motions while on the court at times. This is as close to a medical assessment as we get in the piece, and it's devastating. Cartilage doesn't come back as we age thanks to how blood flow works in the area. That's where things like stem cell therapy come into play. But, at this point, it's pretty clear that after all the miles Steph Curry has logged over the years, we're talking about patching an engine that's getting near the end of its life. Consider this part one of a two-part idea. Part two:

As terrible a setback as the oblique abdominal strain/tear is, this quote plus the one before it really does point to his knee being the ticking time bomb, and that he's well aware that's the case.

The story is that Stephen Curry had the biggest setback of his professional career this calendar year and because his body has started to break down. It doesn't get any scarier than that. This year is almost over. What horror(s) will next year bring?

But I'll end this post … the least scary thing Curry says in the whole piece.

If circumstances demanded it, Curry said he would've been fine sliding into more of a complementary role late in his career, similar to most fading stars. Perhaps he eventually will. "It would not kill my ego," Curry said. "I want to win. Whatever that means, you make decisions based on what's in front of you."

You're not going to find any Stephen Curry followers who don't think the guy has a degree of humility about him. That's part of what makes him special. He might be the greatest. At times, even he might even acknowledge that he's "up there," in terms of the all-time greats. But he's also aware of how fleeting that feeling can be. It won't be long before he's an afterthought. He's certainly been in the league long enough to see opinions, rankings, or simply stature diminish or outright disappear overnight. And there's also the thing where, sometimes, we need to say something out loud just to convince ourselves it's true.

We don't know when Curry will return from his current injury, but there's still just a bit more time left for us to enjoy a bit more history created by his play. If this isn't the last ride, then it's the penultimate one.

#2829. A Lim Kim makes hole-in-one to surge into a 3-shot lead in LPGA season finale

NAPLES, Fla. — A Lim Kim pulled away from a crowded pack in a most spectacular fashion Friday when she made a hole-in-one on the par-3 16th hole and posted an 8-under 64 to build a three-shot lead over defending champion Jeeno Thitikul in the CME Group Tour Championship.

It also helped that Kim picked up birdies on all four of the par 5s at Tiburon Golf Club. She finished with a long two-putt par to reach 15-under 129, the lowest 36-hole score since this tournament moved to Tiburon in 2013.

Nelly Korda, in her bid to win the season finale to get into the LPGA Hall of Fame, shot a 67 and still wound up losing ground. She started three shots behind and now is six back on a course that has been relatively soft with wide fairways that allow for low scoring.

Korda said she has been battling a two-way miss that she is still trying to figure out.

"It gets frustrating because I feel like I have a thought and then I look at my swing and I'm like, 'This is all timing and it's just ...' Yeah, golf is fun sometimes, right?"

It certainly felt that way to Kim, the 2020 U.S. Women's Open champion, who had a calm hand with the putter and delivered one shot that stole the spotlight on a warm, cloudy day. She hit 7-iron from 168 yards that pitched in front of the pin, took one bounced and disappeared.

She stretched out both arms in a quiet, surprised celebration. Kim followed with a 5-foot birdie on the par-5 17th and is halfway home to $4 million prize, the richest payoff in women's golf.

"I needed 155-yard shot, honestly a little strong hit and I make it," Kim said of her ace. "A little luck to me, yeah."

She still has a solid chasing pack behind her.

Thitikul was even par on the front nine and falling behind until she hit her stride late, making five birdies over the last eight holes for a 67 that puts her in the final group with Kim. It was her ninth consecutive round in the 60s at Tiburon.

The 23-year-old Thai has won the CME Group Tour Championship the last two years, she famously finished eagle-birdie last year.

Indeed, the closing stretch at Tiburon is her sweet spot. Thitikul has played Nos. 13-18 at 43-under par for her career — 41 birdies, two eagles, no bogeys and 85% of green in regulation since 2024.

"It might be a positive juju," she said of her success on this course. "I feel like I love to coming back here. I feel like here, the golf course and me are in sync a little bit somehow. Maybe superstitious things, but I feel comfortable to be here.

"You know, last week of the year, what we got in our hand we have to put it all."

The first prize is so big for the LPGA that 24 players in the field have yet to reach $4 million in career earnings. Five of those players were bunched together at 11-under 133, four shots behind. That includes Yuri Yoshida, who won the BMW Ladies Championship in South Korea during the recent four-week swing through Asia.

Also three shots behind was Charley Hull, who won her first LPGA title at this tournament 10 years ago, when the first prize was a mere $500,000.

Ina Yoon (65), Yan Liu (66), Jenny Bae (67) and Auston Kim (67) also were three shots behind. Auston Kim was in the lead until a bogey on the par-5 14th and another bogey on the 18th.

"It's really important to keep your foot on the gas and be aggressive," she said. "There are always opportunities, whether you don't have a good start or it's kind of a quiet start. It's just staying patient and then letting the putts fall when they can."

A soft course figures to get even softer. With adverse weather in the forecast, the LPGA is moving up the starting times Saturday and going in threesomes off both sides for the first time this week.

#2828. As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive

As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.

Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off, prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.

On platform Kalshi, speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.

#2822. ANALYSIS: Day’Ron Sharpe is emerging as a bright spot despite the Nets’ ugly start

Things aren't pretty in Brooklyn right now, not even close.

The Nets are 3-11, and even though the record looks bad, the way they keep losing adds to the frustration. Brooklyn is coming off an embarrassing 137-107 loss to a Chicago Bulls team that entered the game with just two wins.

Beyond that, the team has now lost five games by at least 15 points this season, the most in the NBA. It doesn't stop there, either. The Nets have allowed 135+ points in back-to-back games for the first time since April 1969!

So, yeah, optimism is pretty hard to come by these days. That's to put it mildly, of course.

But for the fearless, ride-or-die fans out there anxiously searching for something, just anything, to feel good about, there is a bright spot worth discussing. That bright spot goes by the name Day'Ron Sharpe.

Sharpe, 25, is the longest-tenured player currently on Brooklyn's roster, in his sixth season with the organization. After the team dealt Nic Claxton to Chicago over the summer in a three-team deal with the Minnesota Timberwolves to bring in Julius Randle, this is Sharpe's first year as the Nets' full-time starting center.

Throughout his career, analytics have always loved Sharpe, particularly for his offensive rebounding. Entering this season, though, the question was more about whether that efficiency would translate to a larger sample size.

And so far, it has continued, and then some. According to Cleaning the Glass, the Nets have been 18.4 points per 100 possessions better with Sharpe on the floor than without him, placing him in the 93rd percentile among all forwards and bigs who have played a minute this season.

While rebounding has always been his big calling card, the biggest difference in Sharpe's on/off numbers seems to come on offense. The Nets have scored 13.0 more points per 100 possessions with the North Carolina product on the court, which ranks in the 95th percentile. It's also the seventh-biggest discrepancy among forwards and bigs.

For perspective, his overall on/off differential currently ranks ahead of notable names like Nikola Jokić (+15.5) and Alperen Şengün (+15.5). He's also just one percentile beyond Karl-Anthony Towns. All three of those players are averaging over 30 minutes per game, compared to Sharpe's 23.6, but that certainly doesn't make it something to scoff at.

Sharpe is no stranger to ranking high in efficiency categories, but the most encouraging part is that he's doing it with an expanded workload so far. Through 14 games, he is averaging over 23 minutes per night. His career high in a single season before this was last year, when he averaged 18.7 in 62 games. So, the big man has never averaged over 20 minutes per night before this season. He's also started all 14 games for Brooklyn this year, already shattering his previous career-high in starts per season, which was just eight in his rookie campaign.

Overall, Sharpe, who re-signed on a two-year, $20 million contract this offseason, has averaged 8.4 points, 7.1 rebounds (including 3.3 offensive boards), and 4.0 assists on 52.9% shooting.

Another encouraging number is the 4.0 assists per game. With Claxton out of the picture, Sharpe has taken on a much bigger role as the offensive facilitator. He's done a really solid job of embracing the responsibility that comes with being an offensive hub. It's a role Claxton anchored for years in Brooklyn.

That's especially important for a Nets team that still seems to be searching for an identity and consistency on offense. The passing isn't necessarily new, either. Sharpe had flashed that in smaller doses throughout his career. Now that he is getting the opportunites, it's becoming even more obvious.

Against the Atlanta Hawks on November 7, he dropped 13 assists and his first career triple-double. The 13 assists were the most in a single game by a Nets center in franchise history.

For me, the biggest concern regarding Brooklyn's squad entering the year was their lack of rim protection after dealing Claxton. That left a big void, and the Nets didn't do much over the summer to fix it. They added Mo Wagner, but as fans have seen, he is much more of an offensive player and that's being kind. That's not to downplay his impact; his offensive ability is certainly important, but he has limitations down low.

It's never been a strength of Sharpe's either. As a result, the team is currently allowing 48.7 paint points per game, the ninth-most in the NBA. For a team like Brooklyn that lacks elite-level firepower and just plain athleticism, it's difficult to win consistently when you're allowing nearly 50 points per game in the paint.

By no means does all of that responsibility fall on Sharpe, though. Sean Marks deserves criticism for structuring the roster that way, and his frontcourt teammates also haven't necessarily helped turn the tide in that facet.

Ultimately, his start to the year has been very promising. Digging deeper than the sheer numbers, the continued efficiency and success while playing at a career-high rate is exactly why fans should be excited moving forward.

There are still 68 games to play, but so far, Sharpe is making the most of his extended role.

#2821. Where the 49ers need to improve defensively vs. Vikings

Last weekend was not a good day for the San Francisco 49ers defense, as they gave up 40 points on the Dallas Cowboys, yet still managed to come away with the 46-40 victory.

San Francisco's defense struggled on all fronts. The secondary especially had its issues, as Dallas's top three receivers all had quality games. George Pickens had 11 catches for 145 yards and three touchdowns, and that was with him dropping three passes. CeeDee Lamb had seven catches for 72 yards and a touchdown, while Ryan Flournoy had six catches for 71 yards and a touchdown.

Cornerbacks Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green, and Upton Stout entered the game banged up, and it showed, as both had their fair share of struggles against Dallas's elite offense. Of course, the matchup wasn't easy facing a high-caliber quarterback with two Pro Bowl receivers, but it was a rough day for a defense that had been quite good over the first half of the season.

That wasn't the only issue. The 49ers pass rush was also ineffective, failing to sack Dak Prescott, and Nick Bosa came out this week and took accountability for his play this season. Bosa has yet to record a sack, although his other numbers still indicate a productive season, especially with the double teams and chips he's facing.

Now, this week, the health is looking better. Stout remained limited in practice with his ongoing shoulder injury and is questionable, but Lenoir wasn't on the injury report and Renardo Green practiced in full on Thursday and is off the injury report for Sunday's game.

But the 49ers still have a tough challenge against the Minnesota Vikings, who put up 30 points on the Green Bay Packers in Kirk Cousins's return. Minnesota's offense suddenly looks formidable, and this battle should be a tough one on both sides.

After their struggles against Dallas, where do the 49ers need to improve defensively against Minnesota? Ahead of Sunday night, defensive coordinator Raheem Morris broke down the main issues he saw from the Cowboys game and what to take from it.

"Extending drives early with some of the penalties to get those guys to go down there, particularly on the first drive [was a problem]. We gave up three, I believe, on that first one," Morris said. "We got the big penalty to get those guys down there. They got a big-time field goal kicker. A couple of big plays in the first half. The two big plays were the ones that killed us there early. Got a pretty good grip on it after that and kind of held it down. It was at some point it was like 38-19. Then that finishing moments, we didn't do a very good job of getting the finishes off. Usually, the finishes happen when you're able to generate pressure with sacks or you're able to get interceptions.

"The Cowboys did a nice job, to give them credit, of getting the ball out of their hand. Did a nice job of getting the ball into their good players' hand, keeping drives going, extending drives. They had about three or four drives there where it was almost like overtime-like play for them, where it was going to be fourth down territory regardless and they were able to capitalize and go down and score on us. You would like to be able to stop some of those plays and be able to get those guys going and get off the grass at those moments and then that score wouldn't have got to where it was, but those things didn't happen.

"We didn't execute that way. And it's a collective group. I know [Nick] Bosa stood up in front of you guys and took all the credit and took all the accountability, but I really think it's just all of us. Some of it could be better play calls for them. Some of it could be better for us, what we can do for those guys. Some of it can be better plays made by us. Some of it, we just ran out a little bit of gas, got a little bit tired. Let's not kid ourselves. Human nature as well. So, fortunate to get out of there with a win. Definitely want to learn those lessons when you get a chance to do those things in those moments, when you get wins. Something that we can learn from and grow from and something that we definitely will."

One thing Morris did see from his team was accountability after the game, with the leaders on the team stepping up.

"They're such an accountable group," Morris added. "Most guys, you come in and you're just upset after a game. These guys, they hold themselves to such a high standard. They come in, they're able to speak very clearly right off the bat. So it's not going to be more vocal the next week because they were vocal the first week. Not necessarily Bosa. Bosa's kind of a to-himself guy, but for a guy like Fred [Warner], he's always going to speak up and do the things that happened. It wasn't like there was mistakes. They did some better job executing. There was a few mistakes. There's always going to be mistakes and there's always correcting mistakes. I'm not saying there's not mistakes, but there's always going to be correcting mistakes, but you correct those mistakes, you move on.

"There's some other things that, just you talking to as an individual player. The best thing about our guys, they always point at themselves first. Whether it's Fred, whether it's Bosa, whether it's DMo (Deommodore Lenoir), Renardo [Green], anybody on our football team. That's the cool part about being here with these guys is they point at themselves first. Then a lot of the times I'm able to say, 'Hey, I can help you here' or 'we can do these things better. We can make these calls. We can help you out, do a little bit better in these situations.' They are all so upfront and forthgoing with those things. That makes it really cool to talk to those guys that way."

Health seemed to be a factor last weekend, but the 49ers do need to be more disciplined and avoid the killer penalties (although some looked to be questionable calls).

But there is a lot at stake this weekend for the 49ers, as their No. 1 seed odds shift dramatically with a win or a loss. San Francisco's offense has always been up to the task, but they'll get their toughest matchup of the year with Brian Flores's defense. So, the 49ers defense will need to show up as well against this new-look Vikings offense with Kirk Cousins and execute on all three levels.

#2812. More Than A Minor League: How The G League Builds NBA Champions

The NBA G League is full of talent, littered with former collegiate stars and former lottery picks. But it's not just a league full of flops who were never good enough for the NBA. It's a launching point for the careers of future NBA champions and a place where struggling NBA players can find their feet and become contributors on an NBA roster once more.

No G League arena knows that story better than the Mississauga Sports and Entertainment Centre. Champions and Raptors of old such as Pascal Siakam, Fred VanVleet, Norman Powell and Chris Boucher once plied their trade on the hardwood at the venue formerly known as the Hershey Centre, before a name change and a changing of the guard saw JaKobe Walter, Gradey Dick, AJ Lawson come through the doors during the era of the Paramount Fine Foods Centre in recent years.

The Raptors have always been at the forefront of using the G League to find contributors and develop their own draft picks, and that should mean something to fans in Mississauga. A lot of folks in other places may scoff at the G League but it is a chapter in the stories of some of Raptors fans' favourite players and, at the bare minimum, a footnote in the 2019 championship.

While fans may know those stories, there are G League alumni littered around the NBA, many of them NBA champions who either got their start in the G or earned their way back to the NBA.

The 2019 Raptors championship team featured two players whose stories are integral to the tale that is 2010s NBA basketball, and both of them got their start in the G and were even teammates at one point in Reno, Nevada, for the Bighorns in the 2010-11 season.

The three-time NBA champion with the Spurs, Raptors and bubble-era Lakers was drafted by Cleveland 46th overall in 2009 after an NCAA championship at UNC, but after 20 games in a rookie year in which he struggled, the Cavs cut him loose, allowing him to move on to San Antonio, where they also waived him. He landed in Nevada with the Reno Bighorns, the former G League affiliate of the Sacramento Kings.

Green balled out in 16 games for Reno, leading the team in scoring with 20 points a night, as well as 7.5 rebounds per game. Arguably most importantly, he shot 43.4 per cent from deep, which was the skill that got him to the NBA and made him valuable there. He just needed a platform to show it.

Jeremy Lin was Green's teammate in Reno, albeit not for long. Lin began his NBA career in Golden State after going undrafted, a tough place to come by playing time as he sat third on the point guard depth chart behind Monta Ellis and some guy named Steph Curry.

Lin spent a lot of time down in the G League with Reno, who had an affiliation with Golden State at the time. He played well and earned himself an opportunity in China during the NBA lockout before returning to North America with the Knicks the following season, and everyone knows how that went for him.

San Antonio Spurs guard Danny Green tries to pull the ball away from Charlotte Hornets guard Jeremy Lin during Monday night's game at Time Warner Cable Arena on March 21, 2016 in Charlotte, N.C. The Charlotte Hornets defeated the San Antonio Spurs 91-88. (Robert Lahser/Charlotte Observer/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

That Reno Bighorns team was a launching point for Lin and Green, but it also had a roster any basketball sicko would love. Steve Novak and Hassan Whiteside suited up for the Bighorns, as did Patrick Ewing Jr, son of the Hall of Fame Knicks big man.

Another multi-time NBA champion, with the Lakers and Thunder, actually began his career with the Oklahoma City Blue, the G League affiliate of the OKC Thunder. His lone season with Oklahoma's G League club led him to a Summer League invite with the Lakers and a Summer League championship alongside Lonzo Ball, Josh Hart and Kyle Kuzma.

Caruso earned himself a two-way contract, which made him the first two-way signee in Lakers history. While on a two-way, he continued to play in the G League with the South Bay Lakers until his talent became so undeniable that he eventually earned himself a regular rotation spot. He's gone on to win two championships and sign $123 million worth of NBA contracts.

While for Lin, Green and Caruso, the G League was where they got their first really meaningful opportunities in professional basketball, for others it has been a platform to resurrect a career that once looked dead in the water. Certain players take longer to find their role and carve out their basketball niche, and the G League can provide an opportunity away from the bright lights of the NBA.

Gary Payton II, son of the Hall of Fame SuperSonics legend, had actually played for the Lakers, Bucks and Wizards before finding his way to the Raptors 905 in January 2021.

With the 905, Gary carved out a role for himself that should be familiar to anyone familiar with the Payton family name: defensive stopper. He won the league's Defensive Player of the Year Award, joining Chris Boucher as the only other player to win the award as a member of the 905. Finding his role in professional basketball during his lone season with the 905 opened an opportunity for him to join the Golden State Warriors, where he won a championship in 2022 and has been an NBA player ever since.

Raptors 905 centre Jamarion Sharp won the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year Award in the G League as a member of the Texas Legends. Who's to say he can't follow in the footsteps of Payton II and carve out a defensive role for himself in the NBA?

While many fans write off the G League as a land of misfit toys and failed prospects, it is anything but that. You are highly unlikely to find future NBA All-Stars in the G League, with the exception of draft picks getting sent down for extra reps, but fans of G League teams ought to be on the lookout for the next elite-level role player like Caruso or Green, because they just might be playing in a G League gym this season.

#2811. Steelers-Eagles preview: What to expect from Philadelphia’s offense, defense Week 11

The Steelers will travel to Philadelphia — a city where they haven't won since 1965 — on Sunday in a game that many fans have had circled as an Eagles victory since before the season.

However, the 2026 Eagles aren't the same team that made the playoffs every year from 2021-25. They enter Week 11 with a dismal 2-7 record, with all those losses coming in a row against the Bears, Rams, Jaguars, Panthers, Cowboys, Commanders and Giants. Philadelphia hasn't been in the win column since a Sept. 20 victory over the Titans.

Is this Eagles team finally bad enough for the Steelers to break such a lengthy losing streak in The City of Brotherly Love? Or will Philadelphia, fresh off a Week 10 bye, be able to hold off the Steelers at home for yet another season? We'll find out in Week 11.

RB: It's been a rough year for the Eagles offense, now on its third quarterback of the season ahead of Week 11's matchup versus the Steelers. The numbers above speak for themselves: Philadelphia has struggled on both the ground and in the air in 2026, dealing with injuries, the sudden retirement of right tackle Lane Johnson, and poor execution from players on the field. The Eagles have only scored over 20 points four times this season, and have yet to break 30 once.

Before a Week 10 bye, the Eagles faced the New York Giants in Week 9, falling 19-11 in an ugly game that's been all too familiar for the Philly faithful. But one thing did change, with the Eagles trying to spark their Jalen Hurts-less offense by replacing backup Tanner McKee with Joe "Bazooka" Milton at quarterback. He's expected to start again against Pittsburgh on Sunday.

The results were not great against the Giants, with Milton finishing with 169 passing yards and 18/34 completion in Week 9. He didn't throw a single touchdown or interception, and was sacked a whopping seven times. However, the guy with the "Bazooka" nickname does indeed have a powerful arm, with Milton logging an 11.8% deep throw percentage along with eight air yards per attempt (both team highs for the Eagles this season). He's also a much better runner than McKee, leading the Eagles with 64 yards on the ground and a 7.1 average against New York.

Frankly, Milton plays like a still-developing quarterback. He holds onto the ball too long and doesn't seem to go through his reads at NFL speed. However, his arm talent does allow him to rifle balls into open zones when he sees them, and there's always a little bit of worry when playing a passer with his physical abilities — even if everything only clicks a few times a game, he can still make defenses pay. It's worth noting that Pittsburgh hasn't played many highly-mobile quarterbacks this year, and has had some issues with deep coverage this season.

With Milton under center, the Eagles have mixed up their playbook from McKee a bit with a few more rollouts and designed quarterback runs. What hasn't changed, however, is that Philadelphia remains an 11-personnel heavy team that likes short throws outside the numbers to move the ball in the passing game. Making matters worse is that despite the short passing game, Philadelphia ranks dead-last in the league in yards after catch in 2026, with just 738 on the year.

First-round receiver Makai Lemon is a name to watch as a twitchy underneath target, and Milton will get to throw to the now-healthy Devonta Smith for the first time this season after the latter missed the Giants game with injury. That's a big boost to what was a decimated Philly receiving core in Week 9. However, Dontayvion Wicks will still be out for the Eagles against Pittsburgh.

Capping the Eagles' offensive ceiling has been a rough year from the line, which lost All-World right tackle Lane Johnson to retirement in October and has struggled with some regression. Jordan Mailata remains a very good left tackle and Philadelphia now has Landon Dickerson back from injured reserve, but the Eagles still rank seventh-highest in sack rate allowed (9%), third-highest in pressure rate allowed (41.9%), and second-highest in runs stuffed percentage (23.5%) despite facing the seventh-most light boxes in the league.

Having inexperienced signal-callers since Hurts landed on injured reserve certainly hasn't helped the Eagles in pass protection. Philadelphia struggled mightily with interior pressure against the Giants, and gave up a number of unblocked rushers on stunts and twists.

One name to watch is rookie right tackle Markell Bell, a massive human being who has struggled some in pass protection this year, but is a promising run blocker.

Still, on the ground, the Eagles' inside zone-heavy attack is tied for 28th in the NFL in yards per rush (3.7), with just 28 non-Milton yards on the ground against New York. However, star running back Saquon Barkley, who played through injury against the Giants, should be rested up after the Eagles' bye and looking a bit more explosive. In two of Barkley's first three games this season, he averaged 5.5 yards per carry — when healthy, the 29-year-old is still a legitimate offensive weapon.

After a nightmare game against the Bengals last week, the Pittsburgh defense matches up much better against Philadelphia. The key will be stifling the Eagles' run game and pressuring Milton, which the Steelers' front seven is certainly capable of, especially with Derrick Harmon back in play on the interior. Milton averaged 3.12 seconds to throw last week — that should give TJ Watt more time to get home against a rookie right tackle.

Still, with Devonta Smith back in the lineup for the Eagles, along with solid ancillary weapons in Lemon and tight end Dallas Goedert available, a Pittsburgh secondary that got torched last week will still need to bring a better performance to the table. That said, there should be a lot more optimism heading into this week than the last for the Steelers' defense.

RP: Much like the Eagles' offense this year, the defensive side of the ball still possesses a lot of talent, but has performed well below expectations. A unit that was the driving force behind a Super Bowl victory just two seasons ago, the Eagles seemed poised to field a young and imposing defense that would keep them contenders for the rest of the 2020s. Instead, they were sellers at the deadline, shipping away defensive tackle Jordan Davis, whom they'd signed to a three-year, $78 million extension this March.

I spoke with Brandon Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation this week, to try to get a sense of why the defense has underperformed, and he said it's been one of the more baffling developments this season. He cited a lingering injury to superstar defensive tackle Jalen Carter and a general lack of pass rush as the biggest factor. Whether or not Carter is living up to the extension he signed this past summer (four years, $152 million) is seemingly a hot topic among Eagles fans and media, but a Steelers offensive line that just lost Mason McCormick should still be plenty concerned about his presence. Even in a "down" year, Carter's five sacks are only two off the NFL lead for defensive tackles.

As a defense, the Eagles' 16 sacks on the season rank 28th, and their 109 pressures rank 26th. According to Next Gen Stats, the Eagles are below league average in blitz rate (26% vs 32%), and in generating pressure, whether that's with the blitz (41% vs 43%) or without (30% vs 33%).

Carter's 20 pressures this season are tied for second on the Eagles behind only Moro Ojomo (22), an upcoming defensive tackle who allowed the Eagles the flexibility to trade away Davis. Jalyx Hunt, a rotational pass rusher who hasn't played more than 43% of the defensive snaps in a game since Week 4, is tied with Carter. Nolan Smith (17 pressures, 5 sacks), Jonathan Greenard (11 pressures, 1 sack), and Zack Baun (9 pressures, 2 sacks) round out the Eagles' underperforming pass rush.

Baun, the Eagles' top off-ball linebacker, is out for the game, the team announced Friday.

With the lack of pressure, the Eagles' secondary has predictably struggled. Third-year nickel corner Cooper DeJean has taken a step back, allowing four touchdowns this season after allowing just one during his first two seasons, and he has nearly as many missed tackles this season (13) as he had in his career (19) before this season. Meanwhile, Riq Woolen remains a volatile corner who has looked like a shutdown player some weeks and like a weak link in others, including surrendering four touchdowns against zero interceptions so far this season.

If there is one bright spot in Philadelphia's secondary, it's cornerback Quinyon Mitchell, who is still performing at a high level. He's allowed just a 55.6% catch rate and a QB passer rating of 76.5 when targeted. Philadelphia has typically let Mitchell stick to one side of the field, but in their most recent game, the Eagles finally tasked Mitchell with shadowing an opponent's number one receiver. Against the Giants, Mitchell followed Malik Nabers and shut down New York's most explosive playmaker.

As for what coverages we can expect from Philadelphia, the Eagles are a team that has lived in both nickel (68% of defensive snaps) packages and single-high safety looks (54% of snaps) for multiple seasons now. That has most typically shown up as Cover-3 looks in zone coverages (36.5%) and Cover-1 in man looks (15.3%).

On the ground, the Eagles aren't quite as bad as the numbers might indicate. While the Eagles' raw run defense totals look poor, they're mostly in the middle of the pack in most metrics, and are surrendering a high yardage per game total mostly because they have been in negative game scripts for much of the season. Philadelphia allows the seventh-fewest average yards before contact (0.81); however, they also allow the eighth-highest average yards after contact (3.33). As a unit, they've missed 43 tackles on running plays, per PFF, but only DeJean (8) and safety Andrew Mukuba (6) are particularly heinous in this regard. No other defender has more than three missed tackles against the run. Philadelphia ranks 15th in stuffed run percentage (17%), but are tied with the Vikings and Patriots for the 13th-most runs of 10+ yards allowed (27).

In theory, the Steelers' strength — running the ball — should fare respectably against this Eagles front. However, the loss of Mason McCormick cannot be overstated. Spencer Anderson takes his spot and has shown a troubling deficiency in play strength and power thus far in his career. He's excelled on the edges as a sixth offensive lineman, where he can take on lighter and less powerful defenders. Having him line up against Carter, though, gives me pause. Meanwhile, the Eagles' secondary should be gettable, but Rodgers has not played well this season. The Eagles haven't gotten pressure consistently, but Rodgers has often found his way into pressure even when the line is holding well. Now, without McCormick, there is potentially an easier path for the Philadelphia defensive line to get into the face of Pittsburgh's mobility-challenged passer.

This could be another frustrating day for the Black and Gold offense.

#2805. Game Preview: Suns chasing their longest winning streak of the season

Who: Phoenix Suns (7-7) @ Utah Jazz (3-13)

Where: Delta Center — Salt Lake City, Utah

Game three of this five-game road trip comes as the Suns head up to Utah. This is their first meeting with this squad this season. Unfortunately for the Jazz, injuries have derailed their season, and they're coming off a worse record than many anticipated. For the Suns, this is no sleepwalk game, but a chance to make a key statement. A win here would give the Suns their longest win streak of the season with three, and could really be the momentum this team needs to reach its true potential.

The Suns, coming off two different wins against the Denver Nuggets and Sacramento Kings, look to keep their road streak clean with zero losses. With a starting five still trying to find its footing, Jordan Ott seems to have solved the issues this lineup faced earlier in the season. The bench, though, continues to look outstanding and deserves a spot in the conversation among the best in the association. With a big game on the line, especially with it being an NBA Cup game as well, the Suns should aim to make this a statement win.

Mark Williams — OUT (Left Shoulder Surgery)

Harrison Ingram — OUT (G League – Two-Way)

Jaren Jackson, Jr. — OUT (Right Knee; MCL Tear)

Lauri Markkanen — OUT (Right Hand Fracture)

Jusuf Nurkic — OUT (R Foot; 2nd Plantar Plate Tear)

The Suns, in their last two games, have run the same starting lineup but have staggered certain players on the bench to make it easier. That has brought some success to this team and is something to watch for in this game. Dillon Brooks has taken advantage of this switch, as it allows him to be aggressive on offense as the second unit's lead scorer. Not only that, but it has helped on defense as well, with him more locked in. We saw this trend in the Kings game with Brooks, and with Devin Booker as well. He had a stint in the first quarter where he was left with just the bench, which let him hunt his shots and let the team take a lead to end the first.

Having key guys like Jordan Goodwin, Ryan Dunn, and Collin Gillespie, who will do anything to find success and win on the court, makes it easier for guys in Brooks and Booker to be the lead offensive guys. Jordan Ott can maintain success by mixing both units, which would help the Suns find another win.

Two things the Suns need to win against the Utah Jazz are the three-point and rebounding game. With no Jaren Jackson Jr., Jusuf Nurkic, or Lauri Markkanen, one of those should be easier than the other. The Suns cannot lose the rebounding game to Mo Bamba, who is trying to revitalize his career, or Jaxon Hayes, who has bounced from team to team. This is a weak frontcourt, and for the Suns, this is the true test for centers Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Malauch. If they are the real deal, they should excel in these matchups and prove they can handle some of the weaker frontcourts.

On the three-point end, they have Keyonte George, who shoots almost 35% from three, with rookie Darryn Peterson also shooting 36%. Mix that with rotation guys like Svi Mykhailiuk and Brice Sensabough, and this Jazz team can erupt at any time from behind the arc. Key shooters Gillespie and Kennard will have to be at their best to match some of the threes this smaller Jazz team will fire off. Brooks and Booker will have to be at their best as well, since they are the two main three-point shooters in the starting five.

The Suns are on the road, so handle this one like the previous one, too. Even if the Jazz court looks funky due to the NBA Cup, their team is going to look even funkier trying to score on a defense that will be bought in. Phoenix extends their longest win streak of the season while also getting their first win in Group A, taking down the Utah Jazz.

#2800. Giants shocked to learn Colts cut ex-teammate Daniel Jones

John Harbaugh's eyes nearly popped out of his head upon learning that the Colts cut quarterback Daniel Jones.

Harbaugh wasn't the Giants' head coach when they stunningly cut Jones in November 2024, so they don't have the personal relationship that Jones maintains with others in East Rutherford. But the Colts are next week's opponent, so the Giants' behind-the-scenes advance-scouting staffers were just thrown a major curveball.

The Colts plan to start first-round draft bust Anthony Richardson, which means an offense that could be more option-based in store on Nov. 29 to hide Richardson's passing inaccuracy.

Daniel Jones has been released by the Colts. Getty Images

"[It changes] probably pretty dramatically. I mean, wow,'" Harbaugh admitted. "I don't want to get ahead of ourselves here, and you just hit me with that. But definitely the offense will be the offense that they run, but it'll be centered around the quarterback for sure, and they're probably different styles to some degree, so we'll have to look at that when the time comes. We have people doing that this week. They'll have to make a left turn, obviously."

Unlike when the Giants demoted Jones from starter to third-stringer to protect themselves against an injury clause in his contract, Jones did not ask the Colts for his release, head coach Shane Steichen said.

In the Giants locker room, news of Jones' release brought back memories. What does it say to teammates when you release the quarterback who started the first 11 games?

"That the writing is on the wall for the season and you have to get through the next six games the best you can play," right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor told The Post. "D.J. is a great guy but he's in such a predicament. He went there last year and balled out, so it's definitely not a 'him' thing. When you trade everyone like they did, it's hard."

John Harbaugh, head coach of the Giants. Getty Images

Giants backup offensive lineman Josh Sills was with the Colts last season and to start 2025. He saw the same hard-working Jones that was beloved by Giants teammates.

"He helped me in any and every way imaginable," Sills told The Post. "He went above and beyond to make sure everyone had what they needed to achieve their goals. It's a team game. It takes 11 guys."

Anthony Richardson will now start at quarterback for the Colts. Getty Images

Next week was billed as the Jones Revenge Game. Instead, Jones didn't even make it through the first year of the two-year, $88 million contract that he signed after a torn Achilles.

Jones might be able to help the Patriots or Ravens in their playoff chase. Or he could help the Eagles not be an embarrassment the rest of the season. Or use his ties to Broncos offensive coordinator Davis Webb to become the backup for a Super Bowl contender.

Any team that claims him off waivers will inherit $2.1 million in salary this season and a $10.5 million injury guarantee for 2027.

Returning to the Giants or reuniting with Brian Daboll in Tennessee are extremely unlikely possibilities.

"I wish the best for him and I know he's going to make the most of his next opportunity," left tackle Andrew Thomas said. "But I'm focused on what we have going on and we're not looking at Indy right now. We're focused on this week and Jacksonville."

#2794. NFL will consider requiring minimum-night stays for international games

After the 49ers and the Rams took dramatically different approaches to their arrival in Melbourne for the first-ever Australia game, we raised the question of whether the league should require teams to get there early enough to advance the goal of promoting American football to international audiences.

Via The Athletic, the NFL will consider adopting a minimum-night stay for teams playing internationally.

“Currently, we leave those football decisions on when the team arrives in the market to the club,” NFL executive V.P. of club business, major events, and international Peter O’Reilly told The Athletic. “It is something that we’ll consider moving forward on: Do we put some minimum nights in a market in there? It’s something we’ll look at.”

The league already does it for the Super Bowl, mandating a full-week experience that includes multiple press conferences, the annual “Opening Night” media extravaganza, and practicing at designated facilities.

“Having access to players and that type of experience when they’re in the market does have a lasting impact,” O’Reilly said. “That’s a factor when you start to think about encouraging or potentially looking at a policy where you’d want a club in the market for more than the day before.”

Beyond impacting strategic considerations, it would add to the total expense. The money would be worth it, if it further enhances the league’s overall reason for going global.

The 6-4 Rams, who are on a bye in Week 11 and play Thanksgiving Eve against the Green Bay Packers, are currently tied for second in the NFC West and have seven more games left in the regular season. McVay did not have a definitive timeline for a return. The team is currently scheduled to play its Week 18 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Jan. 3, a game that could be flexed depending on what the playoff picture looks like at the time.

McVay did not rule out a Nacua return should the Rams make the postseason, but said, "you're planning on not having him."

Luther Burden III (concussion) has cleared protocol after taking a helmet-to-helmet hit in Week 8 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The Chicago Bears wide receiver logged three full practices this week and carries no injury designation. Same goes for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, who was limited this week with a knee issue. "Like 99 problems, but this ain't one," he said.

Injuries that kept him limited in Wednesday's practice did not keep Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers (ankle/quad) away from being on the field Thursday and Friday. The Raiders' leading receiver exited Sunday's loss to the Seattle Seahawks after just 11 snaps with an ankle issue. He is currently listed as questionable.

The Cardinals are preparing to start 40-year-old Josh Johnson against the Chiefs as Carson Beck (beck) sat out Friday's practice. Johnson, who is on his 15th NFL team, would end up being the team's fourth different starter at quarterback in the past four weeks following Beck, Gardner Minshew and Jacoby Brissett.

DeVonta Smith (hamstring) has missed the past three games for the Philadelphia Eagles, but says he's 100% and has felt that way for a while. Smith said he was able to play last week against the Carolina Panthers, but some things are out of his control. He carries no injury designation for Week 11.

#2787. Price beats Kotaskova to become undisputed champion

Lauren Price dominated Michaela Kotaskova to seal her place in history by becoming undisputed world welterweight champion.

Price, 32, took an unanimous, shut-out decision and the acclaim of the crowd to add the WBO title to her collection and become the first Welsh fighter to claim the accolade of holding all four major world titles.

Already an Olympic champion and world champion from her amateur days, it further underlined her claim as being among the very best in boxing.

But the way in which she did it, extending a perfect professional record to 11 wins from her 11 fights, suggested there could yet be more to come.

Price v Kotaskova: Watch undisputed title fight after Edwards v McGregor

History, hunger and headline bills - why Price is box office

Edwards' world title aim to join Welsh boxing greats

Price won every round from every judge in front of a partisan Cardiff crowd, producing an unrelenting pace that punished her opponent at every opportunity.

Although Price could not force a stoppage, there was never any doubt she had done enough against an opponent full of stamina and stubbornness.

Kotaskova, beaten only once, but never stopped in her career, showed real heart but had no answer to Price's expertise.

The Tokyo gold medal winner could celebrate even before the final bell sounded, climbing the corner ropes and into the record books.

It was lapped up by a sell-out Utilita Arena crowd who excitedly acknowledged the achievement and the moment.

Wales has produced 14 world champions, some of them genuine greats.

They include, of course, Joe Calzaghe who so often graced this venue with successful defence after successful defence of his super-middleweight crown.

He never reached undisputed status, though he was able to cross the capital city to go from arena to stadium champion.

That is the next challenge for Price, claiming before she left the ring that more is to come while talk immediately turned to five-weight world champion Claressa Shields as a stadium fight next summer.

That is for the future, but this was a night for history - with the calibre of some of the former boxers in the stands a nod to that.

Champions know champions. Five Welsh world title winners were in the capital to watch their compatriot do something never been done before.

From Cinderella Man Steve Robinson and Barry Jones, to the more recent Joe Cordina, who may still be eyeing a stadium return of his own in the coming weeks.

All have been proud to fly the flag, but perhaps none have worn it quite as much on their sleeve - or shorts - as Price has done.

Here, entering to the strains of a Welsh male voice choir, the atmosphere moved from Friday night in a city centre to full-blooded patriotism.

The anthem stirred so much Kotaskova couldn't help but raise an eyebrow before stepping out of her corner.

From then, she had no time to savour the moment let alone consider become an opportunity the Czech Republic's first world champion.

She felt flurries of punches from the first moments and struggled with the unrelenting pace set by the champion.

Steely-eyed, Price refused to allow a breath and, while Kotaskova continued to try and come onto the front foot, she was met by angry, but calculated attacks.

Kotaskova's problems only increased when she was cut in the fifth round, the hooks from the home fighter providing no let up.

At one point in the seventh, Kotaskova took a shot so fierce she almost turned her back to say no more, but still she came and still Price went hunting with hooks.

She could not find the decisive blow, finally letting the tempo slip, and even enjoying the final seconds as she accepted she had done more than enough to win and win a place in boxing history.

Price was not the only Welsh winner on the night as Rhys Edwards secured a significant victory over Lee McGregor, taking an unanimous decision to claim the WBA Continental featherweight championship.

McGregor, 29, had stepped back down to featherweight after two defeats in his last three bouts and had made it clear he knew his chances of returning to world-challenging level was on the line.

His determination to keep coming forward showed what it meant, soaking up several clean shots, but Edwards proved too quick and too sharp.

The 26-year-old from Penygraig also had something to prove after a disappointing draw with Gully Powar last time out.

Then he faded in the latter round, but here Edwards managed to take McGregor's punches and maintain his own pace. It ensured what is perhaps the biggest win of his career, and to leave McGregor contemplating his options.

Elsewhere on the undercard, Willy Gilheaney's unbeaten record was taken away by the experience of Argentinean Alberto Igancio Palmetta, the former Olympic boxer showing plenty of know-how to overcome the Swansea fighter's guts and early control to take an unanimous points win.

Earlier in the night, Doncaster's Jake Goodwin took the decision in a game middleweight bout with Liverpool fighter Sean Arkwright. Goodwin – who had former world featherweight champion Josh Warrington in his corner – had only accepted the fight on two weeks' notice, accepting before he was even granted time off work.

And there were wins for Welsh fighters Brandon Scott and Kane Shepherd, while Cardigan's Josh Mellor and Newport's Lewis Howells fought to a draw.

#2786. Raiders Week 11: Fernando Mendoza’s arm, legs key against stingy Broncos

With just 186 total points allowed in nine games, the Denver Broncos boast the ninth-best defensive unit in that regard, which will make it tough sledding for the Las Vegas Raiders this Sunday.

The Silver & Black Express rolls into Mile High with a new conductor in prized rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza a road divisional matchup against the first-place Broncos (tied with the Kansas City Chiefs at 7-2 overall). The No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, Mendoza made his first career start against the stifling Seattle Seahawks defense and Las Vegas fell 21-13 in Week 10.

Another formidable defense awaits Mendoza in Week 11 as Vance Joseph's Denver squad comes off a bye week after a wire-to-wire Week 9 26-21 win at the Carolina Panthers two Sunday's ago.

To hear the 23-year-old budding franchise quarterback tell it, however, he wouldn't have it any other way as he preps for his second-career NFL start this Sunday in Denver.

"I believe getting thrown in the fire is the best way to learn, and the Seahawks and the Broncos both have considerably elite defenses," Mendoza said when asked what it's like getting thrown into the fire against two quality NFL defenses. "I really believe every NFL defense is elite because when you're playing at this level, the margin for error is so small, and all the defensive coordinators are geniuses.

"So, I'm honored and blessed to go against a great defensive coordinator in Coach Robbie (Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard) every single day, especially in OTAs and fall camp and training camp. So, I believe that's helped prepare me, an now I'm excited to embark on this journey with my teammates."

How Mendoza settles during his second start against an aggressive Broncos defense bears watching. The Seahawks produced a blueprint of how to and how not to defend the Indiana product last week. When protected with a clean (and sometimes noisy) pocket, Mendoza was a smooth operator going through progressions and using his accurate and strong arm to deliver the football to Raiders pass catchers.

In the first half, Mendoza went 11-of-13 for 90 yards including his first-career touchdown run. When Seattle saw enough of that, head coach and defensive play caller Mike Macdonald went to his bag of tricks of blitz, simulated pressure, and exotic alignments to take advantage of the neophyte signal caller and Mendoza went 6-of-16 for 53 yards in the second half while absorbing six sacks and 12 hits.

Expect Joseph to stick to a similar script and bring the pain on the 6-foot-5 and 225-pound Raiders quarterback. Especially considering the Broncos have 84 quarterback hits on the season alongside 26 sacks. Zach Allen is an ultra-productive defensive lineman who plays both inside as a tackle and outside as an edge rusher and paces Denver with 4.5 sacks and 23 quarterback hits. Edge rusher Nik Bonitto is right there with him with 4.5 sacks and 11 QB hits while defensive tackle Malcolm Roach is disruptive with four sacks and 13 quarterback hits.

Heat-seeking inside linebacker Alex Singleton is a quality clean-up man and is tied for the league lead in tackles at 107 (Raiders inside linebacker Nakobe Dean is who he is tied with) and also has two sacks and six quarterback hits on his stat sheet.

All of this is presented to note Mendoza's accurate arm and fresh legs are integral to Las Vegas' aspirations to walk out of Denver with an AFC West win. That dual-threat ability is essential to counter the Joseph's defense that is every bit as creative and chaotic as Macdonald's group. All it takes is a few successful scrambles to make a defense bite — Seattle did this — and with Mendoza lauded for his cerebral ways and ability to not make the same mistake again, watching the film from last Sunday's loss will showcase just that.

The second-quarter 22-yard dart Mendoza zipped to wide receiver Cody White is an example of this. Mendoza felt pressure, began to scramble but kept his eyes downfield, and his ability to thrown on the arm and velocity on the fast ball were on full display.

"We have a great strength and conditioning staff here, and performance staff as a whole, whether it's the training staff, nutrition, strength. There's so many different aspects of it, so I'm blessed to be a part of it," Mendoza began when as he answered a question about his mobility being an underrated aspect of his game, "I believe I've gotten faster since being here, and I'm grateful for that because in the NFL, those players are fast."

Those fleet feet will come in handy to escape the exotic blitzes Joseph is expected to deploy. Especially with Las Vegas ground game grinding to a halt consistently over the course of the 2026 season, much to the chagrin of Raiders rookie head coach and offensive play caller Klint Kubiak. Mendoza's ability to run helps provide an alternative run game and scrambling for hidden yards and first downs can frustrate the opposing defense.

Kubiak should again go play-action heavy with designed rollouts and bootlegs to vary the launch point of the ball and give his talented rookie cleaner passing lane and run-pass options. Mendoza has the arm talent to push the ball downfield and by getting the ball into the hands of his pass catchers quickly or downfield, Las Vegas can take advantage of Denver's penchant to whiff on tackles as the team has a high 16.2 percent missed tackle rate. Of course, it'd help to have a healthy Brock Bowers available as the tight end is the Raiders' de facto WR1.

Mendoza is keen on balancing staying in the pocket and winning with this arm while also knowing when to run and gain positive yards against Denver.

"There were a lot of moments in the game that we reviewed after in the film, whether it's Coach Kubiak, Coach (Andrew) Janocko or Coach (Mike) Sullivan, they made comments on whatever the situation was, whether it was some inefficiency or a play that in the future we want to change. So, I'm taking those day by day and trying to improve on them," Mendoza said regarding staying in the pocket longer to deliver a throw instead of taking off as quickly as he did in his first start.

While the Broncos boast the ninth-best red zone defense — teams have visited the space between the 20-yard line and end zone 29 times for only 15 touchdowns for a 51.7 percent conversion rate — they are susceptible to getting yards piled upon them allowing 3,195 yards for 27th most amongst the 32 teams.

That right there is a textbook example of a bend-but-not-break defense.

Sunday's Mile High tilt marks the 134th time the Raiders and Broncos go toe-to-toe. The Silver & Black lead the all-time series 73-58-2 (72-5702 in regular season play, 1-1 in the playoffs) but are riding a four-game losing skid against the Horsemen. The last time Las Vegas beat Denver was in January of 2024, a 27-14 victory inside Allegiant Stadium. Since that tilt, the Broncos have won the next four meetings 34-18, 29-19, 10-7, and 24-17. The pair of longtime AFC West foes will meet again in Week 15 in Las Vegas.

"We were in a zone, it was an extended play, and expecting a quick throw and it became something — when extended plays happen, we always talk about the second play, and plaster, and those types of things. Anytime something doesn't go well I wish I would have called something different."

—Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard on Seattle Seahawks wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba's 71-yard touchdown on a broken play

"I think with Brock (Bowers) and anyone in the tight end, wide receiver, anyone, they're constantly talking and as they grow and mesh together it's something that will continue to benefit us as an offense."

—Las Vegas Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko on the chemistry between pass catchers and quarterback Fernando Mendoza

#2783. Colts officially place Daniel Jones on waivers

Daniel Jones is officially on the waiver wire.

The NFL transaction report has gone out this afternoon, and Jones appears as a waiver from the Colts. After the trade deadline, every player who gets released by his team has to go on waivers before he becomes a free agent.

That means any team that wants Jones on his current contract can claim him, but that is extraordinarily unlikely to happen. As the waiver transaction notes, Jones is a vested veteran with a fully guaranteed salary for the rest of this season. No team is going to want to claim that salary.

Once he clears waivers, however, he’ll be an unrestricted free agent, free to sign with any team, and it won’t be surprising if some team wants to add him for veteran depth. Jones has been terrible this season, but he’s been a competent starter at times in his career, and a team that wants an experienced backup may be interested in signing him for a minimal salary.

Jones was also waived almost exactly two years ago, on November 22, 2024. He cleared waivers and signed with the Vikings’ practice squad before signing with the Colts after that season.
