#2775. Brandon Ingram expected to make season debut for Clippers on Monday vs. Rockets

Brandon Ingram is expected to make his 2026-27 season debut for the Los Angeles Clippers on Monday against the Houston Rockets, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

Before opening training camp, the Clippers announced that Ingram had been diagnosed with a partially torn Achilles tendon in his right leg. The partial tear was discovered while the two-time All-Star underwent surgery to remove a bone spur from his right heel in May.

That heel injury caused Ingram to miss Games 6 and 7 of the Toronto Raptors' first-round playoff defeat to the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Ingram was traded by Toronto to the Clippers as part of a package including Gradey Dick, unprotected 2031 and 2033 first-round selections, a 2027 first-round swap and second-round picks in 2030 and 2033 in exchange for Kawhi Leonard.

The deal was originally agreed upon in late June and expected to become official on July 6 when the NBA's moratorium on transactions ended. However, the trade was put on hold amid the NBA's investigation into the Clippers allegedly evading the league's salary cap while signing Leonard to a three-year, $103 million free-agent contract in July 2019.

Both the Clippers and Raptors agreed that the trade wouldn't be completed until the league's probe was completed. The deal finally went through in mid-September, approximately two weeks before NBA teams opened their training camps.

The Clippers knew about Ingram's Achilles tear — repaired in the same procedure that removed his bone spur — before agreeing to the trade, according to interim president of basketball operations Trent Redden. Redden told reporters that Ingram would require about six fewer months of rehab with a partial tear and expected he would play for the Clippers this season.

Ingram averaged 21.5 points, 5.6 rebounds and 3.7 assists for the Raptors last season after being acquired from the New Orleans Pelicans in early 2025. Shortly after joining Toronto, he signed a three-year, $120 million contract extension.

#2772. Cowboys changing things up in search of consistency vs. Titans

Both the Dallas Cowboys, and their closest division rival this season, the New York Giants, host opponents from the AFC South this weekend. If the Cowboys were even living up to half of the expectations of this season, this Week 11 schedule would look like a golden opportunity to separate from the Giants, as they face the 7-2 Jacksonville Jaguars while the Cowboys have the 1-8 Tennessee Titans.

Instead, the Cowboys already blew an opportunity to win in the same week the Giants lost against the San Francisco 49ers. Even if the Giants do lose as home underdogs to the Jaguars, the Cowboys have invited enough added drama this week with a change of defensive play-callers to make the Titans feel like another handful of an opponent.

This is especially true considering how close both other games against AFC South foes have been this year, both in the win column, but neither convincing. Getting a convincing win is something Cowboys fans simply do not have faith in their team doing at all right now, and not something the Titans have given away easily despite struggling under the new coaching of Robert Saleh and offensive coordinator Brian Daboll.

Hope for the playoffs will still feel thin even with a win Dallas is expected to get against these Titans. The Cowboys have made their bed with this roster and coaching staff and will have to withstand however many embarrassing losses can come from it, with the Titans having the potential to be the worst of 2026.

It is time for our weekly look at how the Cowboys avoid this loss and go into Thanksgiving with a chance at a winning streak again, or what could lead to the latest AT&T Stadium embarrassment after all.

Every other week for the Cowboys passing attack seems to feel like a CeeDee Lamb feature game right now, with Lamb having a big say in the win over the Colts in week nine, but it was George Pickens' best game of the season with three touchdowns in week ten agaisnt the 49ers.

The fact we are still waiting into late November for a game where both Lamb and Pickens are established in a game plan and get going at the same time is a horrible sign for play-caller Brian Schottenheimer. Beating bad AFC teams is one thing he's proven capable of though, and if now isn't the time to see both Lamb and Pickens unleashed downfield, it may never come.

The Titans defense is effectively tied with the Las Vegas Raiders for worst in the league in yards per passing attempt allowed. All three of their cornerbacks that led the team in snaps last week against the Jaguars are new to the team this season – Cor'Dale Flott, Alontae Taylor, and Joshua Williams.

Tennessee is also the fourth worst team at getting to the quarterback this season with 14 sacks, just one more than the 49ers team the Cowboys offense scored 40 points against last week. The Cowboys defense is more of an unknown than ever before coming into this game after already underperforming all season, so the adage that Dallas can win this game by having Dak Prescott simply outplay Cam Ward by a big margin is not a reliable one.

That said, another huge Prescott game against this opponent where he's able to effectively get the ball deep to both of his top receivers should be enough to get in the win column. The Cowboys have beaten Robert Saleh defenses consistently before, and will have to do so again to keep faint NFC East hopes alive this Sunday.

The football gods always seem to work in mysterious ways, in the sense they will test the very thing a team is struggling with in the blink of an eye. The Cowboys reasoning for having the veteran coach Mike Pettine take over defensive play-calling from rookie Christian Parker has more layers than an onion. One of the more sound reasons though is that the team is heavily invested financially in their front seven, where Quinnen Williams has looked more and more like a cornerstone player to build around each week in his first full season with the team.

Pettine will likely look to run the defense with a front-centric mindset, focusing on this front seven first and then the backend, where as Parker was the opposite. For a coach that wasn't here for any offseason activity at all, and only been in the building since October, his first test of this new approach comes against a challenging opponent.

With last year's first overall pick Cam Ward at quarterback, the Titans rank in the 98th percentile in their utilization of the quick passing game this season. They have yet another dual-threat, home run hitting running back in former Cowboy Tony Pollard. Ward's best trait has always been his ability to throw the ball out of a moving pocket, and the Titans are figuring out in real time how to protect him and also target the middle of the field at a high rate to open up the sophomore passer's game.

The Titans lone win this season came in week six against the Colts, but this is what Ward's passing chart looked like:

For comparison, the Titans didn't beat the Jaguars last week, but they put up numbers offensively and played well, and this is how Ward threw the ball to do so:

If Mike Pettine is going to make a difference for the Cowboys after they just allowed a franchise record for yards given up in a home game, to a 49ers team that exposed them in the middle of the field, with a mobile QB as well, doing so against the Titans would actually be a solid start.

With the ball coming out so quickly from Ward's hands, the Cowboys likely can't rely on the pass rush element they got against the 49ers with five sacks either. Pass rush will have to come from sound coverage in the short to intermediate part of the field, where the Titans will look to stress Shemar James, Caleb Downs, and even Rashan Gary who got up field without contain on a number of big 49ers plays last week.

If the Cowboys cannot handle these things, and also struggle to get multiple bodies to Pollard in the run game and allow him to get around the edge or push the pile, it could be yet another long afternoon for Brian Schottenheimer's team against an inferior opponent.

#2770. Dustin May’s Four Rings Prove Baseball’s New Reality

Dustin May has four World Series rings, and that number is now shared only with Mookie Betts among active players. The former Dodgers pitcher reached this milestone after helping the Milwaukee Brewers eliminate Los Angeles in the 2026 National League Championship Series.

"It's crazy to fathom that I have four rings," May said. "It's kind of something that not many people in this world have ever accomplished and it's crazy to even think that my name is attached to that."

May's path to the fourth ring was filled with physical pain and unexpected twists. He sat out the full 2024 campaign while healing a torn flexor tendon located in his right arm. An esophageal tear resulting from a freak accident involving a salad required surgery, making things worse. Despite missing time, he still earned a championship ring for the 2024 campaign. Once he resumed playing as a workhorse for the Dodgers during 2025, the Boston Red Sox acquired him at the deadline. He was credited with another ring that season despite leaving the team early.

A winning performance with Milwaukee during the second half of the 2026 season probably increased his market value this winter. After securing a three-year, $52.5 million contract in free agency, May now is a pitcher for the Chicago White Sox. This contract shows that teams still pay big for proven winners, even when their recent history includes major injuries.

While May celebrates, other players struggle with the pressure that comes with winning and losing. Walker Kessler, who plays for the Los Angeles Lakers, recently discussed how scrutiny can ruin the joy of sports. He noted that some players enter the league loving the game but get blinded by the extra noise. "So they lose the love of the game because they focus so much on all the other stuff, and it's sad to see," Kessler said on The Old Man and the Three podcast. May seems to have avoided that trap, keeping his focus on the work rather than the noise. His four rings stand as proof that the game can still be enjoyed if the player stays true to the grind.

#2768. Brandon Ingram expected to make season debut soon with Clippers

Brandon Ingram is set to make his season debut with the Los Angeles Clippers on Monday, Nov. 23, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

The Clippers will play the Houston Rockets at the Toyota Center in Houston on Monday.

Ingram had been working his way back from right heel surgery he had in May. The two-time All-Star also had a partially torn Achilles tendon.

Ingram was initially supposed to have a bone removed from his heel, but the doctors found the partially torn Achilles during that procedure.

Earlier this month, Ingram told reporters that he was "pretty close" to returning and had been on the court a bit more.

He also stated that he had not played any 5-on-5 during the summer but has since been "gaining that confidence."

The Clippers acquired Ingram as one of the primary trade assets in the package sent over by the Toronto Raptors for Kawhi Leonard during the offseason.

Ingram has remain close with the team since his arrival.

He took some time to praise his teammates despite the Clippers' slow start to the season. L.A. has a 4-10 record through the first 14 games.

"I actually want to commend those guys because everybody is in new positions and asked to do more," Ingram told reporters earlier this month. "So the guys are trying. They're playing really, really good defense."

The Clippers fell short in a 124-112 loss to the San Antonio Spurs, in what was a competitive game considering both teams are on opposite sides of the standings.

Ingram return would be welcomed, especially on the offensive end of the floor. The All-Star led Toronto with 21.5 points and was third in rebounds (5.6) during the 2025-26 season. He started 77 games for the Raptors.

"They're trying to figure it out on the offensive end," Ingram told reporters. "When I come in, I want to play make, make it a little bit easier for guys to catch and shoot, and not have to make so many decisions. And be able to, when it gets down to it, be able to score."

Ingram already had a level of familiarity with head coach Tyronn Lue and assistant coach Jeff Van Gundy from playing for Team USA during the 2023 FIBA World Cup.

The Clippers had several players injured to start the month, including Ingram, center Yanic Konan Niederhäuser and Max Strus.

The trio was recalled on Nov. 2 and participated in a weekend assignment with the team's G-League affiliate.

Strus returned to the team after recovering from a partial tear to his right plantar fascia. Konan Niederhäuser made his season debut on Nov. 19 against the Clippers, after recovering from right Lisfranc surgery.

Bradley Beal (right knee injury management) and Jordan Miller (left rotator cuff surgery) will remain the only Clippers without a timetable to return.

#2767. Capitalizing on motion and play-action inside the Jaguars offense

The Jaguars' offense has been exceptional this season. That's not really a secret.

Seemingly anything and everything Liam Coen implements strikes gold.

Among those things is the Jaguars' success with motion, play under-center, and with play-action.

In 2026, Trevor Lawrence is seeing career-highs in use of motion (75.2%), play under-center (45.7%), and play-action (26.8%). The Jaguars just so happen to be about the best team in the NFL in all three departments.

Jacksonville's use of motion over the years is a confusing one. Former head coach Doug Pederson stayed pretty consistent in his use of motion, despite the league seeing a dramatic uptick.

In 2024, his final season in Jacksonville, the Jaguars ranked 31st at just 47.9%.

Since then, Liam Coen has nearly doubled that figure in two seasons. The Jags are now seeing pre-snap motion on 75% of snaps, the fourth-highest mark in the league.

As a whole, the team ranks third in yards per game (281.3), third in yards per play (6.2), and second in EPA per play with motion.

It's no surprise then to see Lawrence has the second-most passing yards in the league with 1,613 yards. On the ground, the Jags rank sixth in yards (873) when utilizing motion.

From under-center, Trevor Lawrence is completing 73.3% of his passes for 665 yards, six touchdowns, zero interceptions, and an NFL-best 142.7 passer rating.

His 11.08 yards per attempt, 73.3% completion rate, 63.3% success rate, and +0.59 EPA per play all rank either first or second in the NFL.

The Jags' ability to run the ball from under-center certainly helps the cause.

Bhayshul Tuten ranks fifth in the NFL with 509 yards gained from under-center, according to Fantasy Points.

It's that success that makes the Jaguars' use of play-action so deadly, a new tool at Trevor Lawrence's disposal.

When using play-action, Lawrence has completed 72% of his passes for 797 yards, six touchdowns and zero interceptions, and another NFL-best passer rating of 133.0. He again is Top-2 in yards per attempt (10.6), success rate (64%), and EPA per play (+0.552).

It's this marriage of coaching and talent between Liam Coen and Trevor Lawrence that has made this Jaguars' offense so scary. Yes, Trevor Lawrence is playing the best football of his career and maybe in the entire NFL.

But, it's also true that Liam Coen is using anything and everything at his disposal to put Lawrence and the rest of his players in the best position to succeed.

#2766. Daniel Jones has been released by the Colts. Should the Patriots go after him?

You heard about a Friday news dump, but have you heard about a Friday QB dump? That's precisely what the Indianapolis Colts did when they released their starting quarterback, Daniel Jones, earlier today.

Jones, 29, was in his second season with the franchise and just eight months removed from signing a two-year, $88 million contract extension. However, he and the Colts as a whole have struggled mightily this year, leading to some sweeping changes within the organization. First, they fired the GM who signed him to that deal, Chris Ballard, and now they let go of Jones himself.

His release comes with the Colts at 3-8 and Jones having completed 205 of 351 pass attempts (58.4%) for 1,974 yards with seven touchdowns and 13 interceptions. A year removed from tearing his Achilles tendon, he is ranked 30th among 31 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA per play this season (-0.139) and 31st in both net yards per attempt (4.8) and completion percentage above expectation (-6.1).

Long story short, he has been dreadful. And yet, the New England Patriots might just keep a close eye on him.

The Patriots, after all, saw their own starting QB, Drake Maye, suffer a fractured fibula during last Sunday's loss versus the Detroit Lions. While it remains to be seen how long he will be out, Maye missing most if not all of his team's seven final regular season games this year would not come as a surprise.

The question now becomes whether or not the Patriots should pursue Jones as a replacement. Let's make the argument in favor of and against such a move.

Before making this argument, it needs to be prefaced with this: everything in this section only applies to Jones going through the waiver wire unclaimed and making it to the open market. According to Jason Fitzgerald of Over the Cap, a team would need $6.35 million in salary cap space to claim Jones — financial flexibility the Patriots do not have at the moment. If he passes waivers, he could be signed to a deal worth as little as $505,554.

With that out of the way, let's take a look at why brining Jones in would make sense for the Patriots. It all starts with one question: would he be an upgrade over Tommy DeVito for however long Drake Maye will be sidelined?

His play this season so far suggests that that might not be the case. However, a change in environment might help Jones regain some of the confidence he had in his first year with the Colts, when he played some of the best football of his career and finished the season sixth in the league in EPA per play (0.201). If the Patriots can get a fraction of that, they should be happy with Jones as a better alternative than DeVito.

In addition, Jones also has some familiarity with the Patriots scheme. While he never played directly under offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, he did spend the better part of three seasons under former New England assistant Brian Daboll. The offense Daboll ran with the Giants has similarities to McDaniels' in terms of terminology, quarterback responsibility and play designs, meaning that the lead-up time for Jones to get ready would be comparatively small.

Inserting Jones would likely also not come with significant philosophical changes. In essence, after all, he is a similar player type as Maye is: somebody capable of making plays with his arm as well as his legs, as evidenced by his career rushing average of 6.1 yards per carry.

While his highs have not been close to Maye's, he has shown that he can be an adequate NFL starting quarterback and somebody able to elevate the talent around him. That obviously was not the case in Indianapolis this season, but if a change of scenery and move to a better-run team can get him close to that, it would be precisely what the Patriots need right now if there are any doubts about DeVito.

And even if not, what do the Patriots have to lose? They are 5-5 and fighting for their playoff lives, and signing Jones would not automatically disqualify them from starting DeVito. At the very least, he would provide veteran depth better suited to challenge the post-Maye hierarchy than sixth-round rookie Behren Morton.

On Friday, Jones became the first quarterback in the NFL in more than three decades to get released less than 24 hours after starting a game. That plus the fact the Colts are willing to cut their losses despite the financial investment they made in him just this offseason should tell you all you need to know.

While there might be a snowballing effect to Jones' struggles and a fresh start could indeed help him regain the form he previously showed, there is no denying he has played some of the worst football in the NFL this year. The numbers mentioned above are an illustration of that.

Some of it had to do with the surroundings and a Colts team that a) lacking quality across the board, and b) is in a free fall since October. In addition, his injury situation also seems to have played a part in it: 12 months after his torn Achilles, he still does not look like he is close to 100% and fails to consistently to step into throws, maneuver the pocket and pick up yards on the ground, averaging just 3.8 yards per carry.

On top of it, Jones has been a streaky player throughout his career. While there have been stretches of play where he lived up to his former first-round status, the lows have been underwhelming, including this season.

Given all of that, expecting a quick turnaround in New England would be naive, particularly considering that the Patriots are missing several offensive pieces because of injury. But even if they didn't, Jones would not have any familiarity with them: despite some experience in a McDaniels-style system, he would have to build chemistry with his receiving corps, offensive line and coaching staff on the fly.

Tommy DeVito, meanwhile, has a two-year head start in that regard. Speaking of DeVito, he was signed to a contract extension in the offseason to serve as QB2 and has, by all accounts, been a model citizen deserving of his shot. Obviously, the job should go to the best option regardless of contract situation. That said, all things considered — including what a change might mean for the locker room — DeVito still has a strong case to be just that.

Even though they are still in a competitive position on paper, the Patriots are fighting for their playoff lives with Drake Maye sidelined for the foreseeable future. Their margin for error, meanwhile, is, to quote safety Kevin Byard, "basically at zero."

Would adding Jones increase it and allow New England to play winning football during Maye's absence? Ideally, that is not a question they would have to ask; Tommy DeVito stepping in and leading the offense at an adequate level would be the best-case scenario. Of course, as the Lions game showed, there is a realistic chance the lights are too bright for him.

The problem is, they also might be for Jones. So far this season, after all, he has not been good and not been able to hold up to the pressure of being the guy at quarterback in Indianapolis. He wouldn't quite be that in New England, sure, but the eyes of one of the NFL's biggest markets would still be on him.

Would that prevent the Patriots from signing him? Probably not. Still, it is one of the factors to consider alongside the arguments outlined above. And putting all of those together, it is clear the decision whether or not to sign Jones as a potential stand-in for Maye is quite nuanced. At the end of the day, Mike Vrabel, Eliot Wolf and Ryan Cowden — the latter of whom spent time with Jones in New York — will have to see their way through it.

And once they do, they very well might find that the potential disruption caused by adding Jones might not be worth the theoretical gains.

What do you think about Daniel Jones? Should the Patriots pursue him, or steer clear of him? Please head down to the comment section to share your thoughts, or jump into the following discussion thread set up by community member Gonzucla in the Feed.

#2764. Things look bleak for Warriors, but they can survive this

The Warriors are in free fall, losing five games in a row, including their last four by 20 or more points.

Golden State Warriors guard Stephen Curry, right, confers with head coach Steve Kerr during an NBA game in Denver, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. AP Photo/David Zalubowski

Of the 15 Western Conference teams, only 11 are going to have a real shot at securing the 10 playoff spots unless something drastically changes.

In other words, the West cellar is so weak that even if the Warriors can't arrest their precipitous slide without Steph Curry, they'll have more than enough time to recover when he returns.

So, while what's happening to the Warriors is unfortunate, it's far from catastrophic.

Curry is expected to be sidelined close to a month after suffering a right oblique abdominal tear on Nov. 11.

The 38-year-old had carried the Warriors to eight straight wins while playing some of the best basketball of his career, averaging 27.8 points (50% shooting from the field, 45.7% from beyond the arc), 3.7 rebounds and 3.9 assists per game.

Before Curry sustained the injury, he and Yaxel Lendeborg were looking like one of the NBA's best duos. Lendeborg, whom the Warriors drafted with the No. 11 overall pick in June, was having a Rookie of the Year campaign, averaging 21.6 points on 52.2% shooting.

But with defenses collapsing on him without Curry, the rookie has wilted, averaging 13.7 points on 26.8% shooting over the last four games.

Not only is Curry going to be back in the lineup soon, but Jimmy Butler (torn right ACL) is expected to return midseason.

The Warriors could still be really good. They could still have a deep playoff run. They could still be a contender.

This has been a roller coaster for Warriors fans.

Entering the season, it was questionable whether the Warriors would make the playoffs after they pretty much stood pat during the offseason. And after dropping their first three games, it seemed all but guaranteed that this was going to be a wasted season for Curry, a two-time MVP who carried the Warriors to four championships in eight years from 2015-2022.

Lendeborg emerged as his sidekick. He sprinted past his expectations. He became a force.

Yaxel Lendeborg, left, and Golden State Warriors head coach Steve Kerr smile during a game against the Houston Rockets on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in Houston. NBAE via Getty Images

All of a sudden, Curry and Lendeborg were stomping on their competition, beating contenders such as the Lakers, Timberwolves and Nuggets over a stunning stretch that had pundits questioning whether the Warriors were championship contenders.

But the short-handed Warriors were always one Curry injury away from disaster.

And when their nightmare was realized, the Warriors went from being one of the league's most fun teams to one of its biggest duds.

Golden State Warriors head coach Steve Kerr watches play during an NBA game against the San Antonio Spurs on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in San Antonio. AP Photo/Darren Abate

Curry and Butler will return, and the Warriors will have more than enough runway to correct course.

So the excitement the team was generating a little over a week ago?

#2763. Las Vegas Raiders-Denver Broncos FEED Topic: Kolton Miller, DJ Glaze vs. Nik Bonitto, Jonathon Cooper

The Seattle Seahawks managed to get six sacks on Fernando Mendoza in his starting debut last week, and pressure on the quarterback will be another major key to the game for the Las Vegas Raiders' offense in Week 11. The Denver Broncos present the same problem but in a different way than Seattle, one that will place a greater emphasis on the Raiders' offensive line, especially tackles Kolton Miller and DJ Glaze.

Led by head coach Mike Macdonald, the Seahawks defense uses a creative scheme to help manufacture pressure and create confusion for opposing quarterbacks. To a certain extent, they're able to work around or neutralize the offensive line by attacking running backs in pass protection or forcing quarterbacks to account for free rushers by throwing hot. Last week was a perfect example, as top cornerback Devon Witherspoon led the team with two of the six sacks.

Meanwhile, Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph isn't afraid to blitz, but that's to help create one-on-one opportunities for their defensive linemen, especially edge rushers Nik Bonitto and Jonathon Cooper.

Bonitto is coming off back-to-back Pro Bowl seasons, where he registered 27.5 sacks and 133 pressures, per Pro Football Focus, in 2024 and 2025 combined. This season, he's recorded 4.5 sacks in nine games and ranks tied for 19th among edges with 30 pressures.

Meanwhile, Cooper notched 18.5 sacks and 112 pressures in the two previous seasons to give the Broncos a quality No. 2 pass-rusher on the edge. In 2026, he's only participated in three games due to off-field issues in the offseason and has just 10 pressures and 0.5 sacks on 77 pass-rush snaps. So, Cooper's numbers are down as a consequence of his actions, but his track record on the field speaks for itself.

On the other side of the trenches, Miller has an impressive resume in pass protection but has been regressing this year. With 32 pressures on 379 opportunities, per PFF, his 8.4 percent pressure rate is the highest it's been since the 2018 first-round pick's rookie year (11.0 percent). But Glaze is trending in the opposite direction, going from 8.3 percent and 8.0 percent pressure rates in his first two seasons, respectively, to 4.0 percent (15 pressures on 379 opportunities) this year.

With the Raiders shifting from Kirk Cousins to Mendoza last week and seeing their playoff hopes rapidly decline over the last roughly two months, we've reached the point in the season where it's time to start looking at building for the future. Part of that is making sure the rookie quarterback can stay upright enough to make some plays and build confidence heading into next year. The other part is evaluating the team's needs before the offseason gets going.

It would be remiss to talk about the Broncos' pass rush and not mention Zach Allen, who currently leads all defensive tackles with 38 pressures and has 4.5 sacks. However, it feels like a foregone conclusion that Las Vegas will have to address its guard situation this spring. Meanwhile, offensive tackle is still up in the air, and this weekend will be a good litmus test for Miller and Glaze.

Is the veteran left tackle past his prime, where it's time to find a new blind side protector? Is the third-year pro's growth legitimate? How they fare against one of the NFL's best edge-rush duos over the last few years, Bonitto and Cooper, on Sunday will go a long way toward answering those questions.

So, for this week's game day discussion on The FEED, we'll be keeping tabs on how well Miller and Glaze can protect the edges to keep Mendoza clean in Denver. The game kicks off at 1:25 p.m. PST and will air on CBS (check your local listings). I look forward to talkin' some ball with y'all!

#2759. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2754. Championship hangover? Josh Hart 'not in a good headspace' as he, other Knicks struggle amid uneven start

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Knicks slipped to 6-6 on Friday with a 106-104 loss to the Indiana Pacers, dropping into a tie for fifth in the Eastern Conference alongside the Miami Heat.

While it hasn't been an outright disaster of a start, it has been an uneven performance by the defending champions that has left them frustrated and searching for answers. The championship hangover in New York seems to be real, and the once immaculate vibes at Madison Square Garden have been replaced by frustration as they try to get on track.

After a scoreless performance against the Pacers, Josh Hart was brutally honest about not knowing what's wrong and how he's been struggling mentally to start this season.

"Wish I could tell you," Hart said. "Don't know. Right now I'm not in a good headspace, and I got to figure out how to improve that and improve my play."

One of the strengths of the Knicks during their title run last year was their rotation of two-way wings between Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns, but so far this season their three best wings -- OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Hart -- have been stuck in the mud offensively.

Those three are all shooting below 40% from the field and below 33% from 3-point range this season, a massive departure from last season when they were all above 48% from the field and 37% from distance. The result of New York's wings struggling on offense -- aside from Landry Shamet, who has been a needed bright spot -- has been an even greater burden on Brunson and Towns.

Towns has been sensational, averaging 21.1 points and 13.7 rebounds per game on 54.2/40.0/77.0 shooting splits as he's moved back to a full-time role at center after the departure of Mitchell Robinson. Brunson has been his typically excellent self, averaging 26.6 points and 5.7 assists per game -- a slim uptick in points and a small decrease in assists from last year -- but his efficiency has dipped, shooting 43.6% from the field.

While his 3-point percentage has held firm at 37.5%, he's shooting just 55.8% from inside three feet. That would be the worst finishing rate of his career at the rim and seems to be a byproduct of teams collapsing in without the threat of spacing from the wings around Brunson.

A less effective Brunson at the rim, the struggles of their wings and Towns playing more at the five have resulted in a Knicks offense that is 29th in the NBA in paint points at 35.5%. Mike Brown's offense is predicated on launching threes, but a year ago the Knicks got 41.4% of their points in the paint. A 6% drop-off there is a significant reduction, especially considering how poorly they're shooting from three as a team.

The big question raised by Hart's comments after Indiana's game is: how did the Knicks get here after winning the title?

It's one thing to have a championship hangover, but it's another to have the vibes of a team sour so quickly, considering their success was built in no small part on being a tight-knit group. It's hard not to point to the top of the organization and the way James Dolan seemed adamant about raining on the Knicks' championship celebration almost as soon as it began.

Dolan didn't even let the champagne-soaked locker room dry out before he proclaimed his refusal to go into the second apron to keep the team together. He stayed true to his word, letting Robinson walk to the rival Boston Celtics. However, what was perhaps more impactful on this year's poor start is the way the Knicks handled extension talks with much of their roster.

Towns made clear his desire to work out a deal to stay in New York and cut the Knicks a hometown discount, but New York was asking him to take an even bigger pay cut than he was willing. Ultimately, talks fell apart and the Knicks made the curious decision to publicly announce they were no longer going to discuss extensions with anyone on the roster a week before the season began.

Hart is among the extension-eligible players, but unlike Towns, who can decline a player option and hit free agency, his option for next year is a $22.3 million team option. If the Knicks wanted, they could simply pick up Hart's option and extend discussions on a new deal into next summer. One can't help but wonder whether the uncertainty about the future is part of whatis affecting Hart and putting him in a bad headspace.

Some players thrive under the pressure of a contract year, while others just feel the anxiety of not having a stable future. Hart, whose impact often goes beyond the box score, might feel that more than others.

The Knicks had two paths they could've taken this summer after winning their first title in over 50 years. One was to do everything possible to lock up the core group as quickly as possible and try to keep the good vibes rolling. The other was to play hardball and use the championship as an opportunity to squeeze players for a discount.

Knicks fans weren't surprised to see Dolan choose option two, and now they have to wonder if that's at the root of an uneven start to their title defense.

#2753. Jacob Misiorowski named National League Cy Young winner: Brewers ace takes home unanimous honors

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski has unanimously been named National League Cy Young Award winner for the 2026 Major League Baseball season. He beat out the Phillies' Cristopher Sánchez and the Braves' Chris Sale.

Misiorowski takes home the honors of the Baseball Writers Association of America vote, which was revealed on Wednesday night. Misiorowski's triumph comes after a stellar age-24 season for the World Series champions:

In addition to the top-line numbers above, Misiorowski struck out 37.9% of opposing batters, which is tops in all of MLB and a sky-scraping figure for any pitcher, let alone a starter. Miz also paced the majors in FIP with a mark of 2.17, and his ERA+ of 232 is the 13th-highest figure by a qualifier ever in MLB. Misiorowski's WAR of 6.4 ranked third in the NL behind Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo of the Philadelphia Phillies.

Misiorowski was perhaps even more notable for his blazing fastball than he was the dominance of his statistical outputs. For the season, Misiorowski averaged 100.6 mph with his heavily used four-seamer, and on multiple occasions during 2026 he threw the fastest pitch on record, including this 105.5 mph offering from June:

105.5 MPH FROM JACOB MISIOROWSKI 🔥🔥 pic.twitter.com/wjvkdc7iWE

While Misiorowski's playoff performance was not part of the Cy Young criteria – ballots are submitted before the playoffs begin – he did post a 1.89 ERA in four starts this postseason for the Brewers, who wound up winning it all for the first time in franchise history.

Misiorowski is now the fourth Brewer to win the Cy Young Award. Corbin Burnes won in 2021, and Pete Vuckovich and Rollie Fingers won in 1982 and 1981, respectively, when the franchise was part of the American League.

Given his level of dominance and relative youth, Misiorowski figures to enter the 2027 season as the odds-on favorite to win the hardware again. If he does, he'll become the first back-to-back Cy Young winner in the NL since Jacob deGrom of the New York Mets in 2018 and 2019.

#2752. Kane out for 'few months' with ankle ligament tear

England captain Harry Kane will be out "for the next few months" after tearing ligaments in his left ankle during Bayern Munich's 1-1 Bundesliga draw with Cologne on Friday.

The striker, who last month won the Ballon d'Or for the world's best player, was forced off after 20 minutes following a challenge from defender Joel Schmied.

The 33-year-old initially tried to continue before being limping off the pitch to be replaced by Tom Bischof.

A Bayern statement said Kane had "suffered a torn syndesmotic ligament in his left ankle" and would "therefore be sidelined for the next few months".

Bayern trailed to a goal from England Under-21 winger Mikey Moore - who is on loan at Cologne from Tottenham - at the time, before they equalised through a Nathaniel Brown goal in Kompany's first game back after a five-game absence.

Kompany had been absent after being diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

Kane's injury comes on the same day England were drawn against Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals, with the two legs on 27 and 30 March.

He had scored for his country in wins against Croatia and Spain this month to help England finish top of their Nations League group, with this being Bayern's first game back after the international break.

Kane has scored four goals and registered eight assists in 10 league appearances this season, while managing four goals and three assists in four Champions League games.

Kane has had a good fitness record since his move to Germany from Tottenham in August 2023, but he does have a history of ankle issues.

He injured his left ankle playing for Bayern in March 2024, prior to an international break, and missed friendlies against Brazil and Belgium.

While at Spurs, the striker was ruled out for two significant spells in the second half of the 2018-19 season, missing seven games when he damaged ligaments in his left ankle and then nine more matches with a lateral ligament injury.

In 2017-18 he missed a month with a similar injury to the right ankle, and endured separate absences of six and four weeks during the 2016-17 campaign.

#2751. Cy Young winners Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler just put up a 2026 tandem not seen since 1905

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

To no one's real surprise, Jacob Misiorowski of the Milwaukee Brewers and Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees have been named the 2026 Cy Young Award winners for, respectively, the National League and American League. Each was announced as the winner of Major League Baseball's topmost honor for pitchers, and each won the balloting in unanimous fashion. They are the first duo to win unanimously in the same year in their respective leagues since Justin Verlander and Sandy Alcantara in 2022 and just the third in MLB history.

Obviously, Cy Young winners have necessarily authored excellent seasons, but in the case of this year's winners, the descriptor "excellent" doesn't quite rise to meet the work of Misiorowski and Schlittler:

We could get into stuff, yes, as each has a blazing fastball that overwhelms hitters at the front end of a deep repertoire. This exercise, though, is more about how Misiorowski and Schlittler have overwhelmed the opposition when it comes to keeping runs off the board. You'll note all the strikeouts above, of course, but what may catch the eye is that each boasts a sub-2.00 ERA. That's a time-honored signifier of pitcher impeccability, even if ERA has its flaws.

To upgrade this familiar stat just a bit – and to put the two 2026 Cy Young winners' accomplishments into fitting context – we'll turn to ERA+. ERA+ is ERA adjusted to reflect league and home ballpark tendencies. An ERA+ of 100 represents the league average, and each point above or below that mark reflects a one-point change. For example, a pitcher with an ERA+ of 120 had a park- and league-adjusted ERA that was 20% better than the league average, while a pitcher with an ERA+ of 95 was 5% worse than the league average. So from the hurlers' standpoint, the higher the ERA+, the better.

This is all a necessary step when comparing pitchers across eras, because run–scoring environments have changed so drastically over the history of the sport. For example, Pedro Martinez's ERA of 1.74 in 2000, when teams were averaging more than five runs per game, means a lot more than, say, Charlie Chech's 1.74 ERA in 1908, when teams averaged 3.38 runs per game. That's where ERA+ comes in. Martinez in 2000 had an ERA+ of 291, or a park-adjusted ERA that was 191% (!) better than the league average. Chech in 1908 had the same ERA as Martinez in 2000, but his ERA+ of 136 was drastically worse.

As for the two moundsmen of present interest, Misiorowski this past season had an ERA+ of 232, which led the majors. Schlittler had an ERA+ of 215, which led the American League. Yes, they had those sub-2.00 ERAs, but, really, topping a 200 ERA+ is a much more impressive achievement. Counting Misiorowski and Schlittler but throwing out the pitchers who achieved the mark in the 60-game 2020 season (you should always throw out 2020), just 43 pitchers in MLB since 1900 have managed a 200 ERA+ or better across a qualifying number of innings. Over that same span and with 2020 also omitted, 201 pitchers have achieved a sub-2.00 ERA in a qualifying number of innings.

As you can imagine, it's a rarity to have not one but two pitchers in the same season who have a 200 ERA+ or better, as was the case this past season with Misiorowski and Schlittler. How rare? No season has ever given us more than two such qualifiers. Here's the full list of those across all of modern MLB history (i.e., since 1900):

Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers (232); Cam Schlittler, Yankees (215)

Jacob deGrom, Mets (218); Blake Snell, Rays (217)

Jake Arrieta, Cubs (215), Zack Greinke, Dodgers (222)

Roger Clemens, Blue Jays (222); Pedro Martinez, Expos (219)

Carl Lundgren, Cubs (211); Jack Pfiester, Cubs (214)

Christy Mathewson, Giants (233); Ed Reulbach, Cubs (209)

Yes, just six seasons have given us more than one 200 ERA+ pitcher, and this year's Miz-Cam combo marks just the third time that we've had one from each league. Accordingly, this marks just the third time that each Cy Young winner has reached the 200 ERA+ benchmark in a given season.

There's another, even more exclusive group that puts the Miz-Cam tandem in the proper context and hints at a future that's as bright as their present and their recent past. In 2026, Schlittler was in his age-25 campaign, while Misiorowski was in his age-24 season. So they're young as frontline aces go, and while you never want to make assumptions about pitcher health and durability in the current era, this duo's elite performance at both top-line and underlying level raises the possibility that each will win another Cy or two (or three) in the years to come.

Turning back to the 200 ERA+ defining stat, such youth in tandem with such excellence is all but unprecedented. Of the seasons listed just above, just 1905 featured two pitchers who, like Miz and Cam this past season, were age 25 or younger at the time. Mathewson, the inner-circle all-time great, was 24 that season and Reulbach was a 22-year-old rookie. We haven't seen something like that in more than 120 years.

Let's also note that Misiorowski and Shlittler, who each struck out more than 30% of opposing batters this season, absolutely have the stuff and foundational, forward-looking results to continue lording over their guild. Until that comes to pass, though, let's appreciate ther historical rare success and their even more historically rare combination of success and youth.

#2748. How Aidan Hutchinson injury could grant Lions a salary cap credit in 2027

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The loss of star edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson, who suffered a season-ending torn ACL while celebrating a sack in Week 10, is a brutal blow to the Detroit Lions in their hunt for the NFC North title and beyond. There is a silver lining to the injury, though. Clauses in Hutchinson's contract and the NFL's collective bargaining agreement with the NFL Players Association open the door for the Lions to potentially gain financial flexibility as a result of his looming absence.

In the massive four-year, $180 million contract extension Hutchinson signed in 2025, there is a clause that permits the Lions to purchase insurance policies against his salary, according to the Detroit Free Press.

The contract reportedly states that the Lions are entitled to purchase insurance policies naming them as beneficiaries for up to $60 million in lost salary if Hutchinson cannot play due to injury. For this season specifically, the Lions may insure up to $45 million. That sum includes $15 million of his signing bonus, the full $28.4 million option bonus and his $1.2 million base salary.

It is unknown whether the Lions purchased those policies and, if so, whether they maximized them.

Not only would the Lions earn a prorated amount of Hutchinson's salary as an insurance payment, but the CBA would also allow them to receive salary cap credits in future years to offset the difference between Hutchinson's pay and the insurance proceeds.

Hutchinson's salary and bonuses still count toward the 2026 salary cap, but the Lions could free up millions of dollars in space for 2027 if they purchased sizable insurance policies. According to Over The Cap, Detroit owns the fourth-most cap space this year at $32.9 million and ninth most in 2027 at $62.1 million. Multiple key players, including tight end Sam LaPorta and safety Brian Branch, will reach free agency at the end of this season, so maximizing 2027 cap space would help the Lions re-sign them to larger contracts.

Salary insurance is expensive, and the Lions do not purchase policies for all players. They reportedly did not insure quarterback Jared Goff's contract when he inked an extension in 2024, nor did they insure linebacker Jack Campbell offseason deal. Campbell suffered a severe neck injury in Week 8, and it is unclear when -- or even if -- he will return to the football field.

Language about salary cap credits for insurance payments first appeared in the CBA in 2006. It took a few years for teams to take advantage of the clause. A CBS Sports report in 2024 found that the New York Giants included an insurance clause in the addendum to Eli Manning's historic 2009 contract extension that made him the highest-paid player in the NFL. And the earliest known instance of a team qualifying for the cap credit came in 2013 when the Green Bay Packers insured $20 million of Aaron Rodgers' $35 million signing bonus.

The Lions have a history of insuring their largest contracts. They did so in 2017, when they took out a policy on Matthew Stafford's five-year, $135 million extension. Interestingly, they did not do the same when they re-signed Goff. And as of Oct. 2024, Goff's contract was the only one out of the 13 quarterbacks who earned an average of $45 million per year or more that was not insured.

Salary cap credits tied to these insurance policies tend to be more modest than one might think. The policies typically require players to miss a certain number of games before payouts begin. Sometimes there is a deductible associated with the policy. This reduces the total payout and, in turn, the amount of cap relief teams receive from the NFL.

#2745. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The big prize of this free agent class is ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. We've seen and will continue to see predictions that he's going to land a deal of around 8-10 years and topping $400 million. The knee-jerk reaction to such prognostications in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the signing team is getting a surefire ace for several years.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here says this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

Also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a new procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. If he signs an eight-year deal, it'll run through his age-37 season.

For those so worried about the long-term finances of the team owner who ends up signing Skubal, are you sure you're really worried that he won't be productive through five, six, seven or even all eight years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

Justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

David Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

By this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:

Are you sure a 10-year, $400 million deal for this guy would be a "risk?"

I think we could argue that it would be a bargain.

#2742. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Celtics win Jaylen Brown trade (for now), Trae Young looks done

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Every now and then, the NBA gives us a week that is essentially built around a single game. A total of 51 games were played in the last week, but come on, the one you remember was Jaylen Brown's long-awaited reunion with Jayson Tatum. The Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers squared off in a battle of the Eastern Conference's two top seeds on Tuesday, and even if the game fell short of our basketball expectations, it provided more than enough beef to sate us. Brown snubbed Tatum before the game. Paul George gave a fan the middle finger. Appropriate animosity has returned to this eternal rivalry.

So... how did we handle that from a winners and losers perspective? Well, Boston is an obvious winner, but Brown escaped loser status. It's winners and losers of the week. Philly won its two other games this week, and Brown led all scorers in Sunday's win with 31 points. He certainly lost on Tuesday. He may yet wind up losing the trade. But we're not docking him a whole week for a single poor performance. So if Brown escaped the loser's section, who made it? And who joins Boston in the winner's circle? Let's look back at the week that was.

Boston's big win over Philadelphia underlined something that's been evident all season: Paul George, at least thus far, has been better as a Celtic than Jaylen Brown has been as a 76er. There are obviously circumstantial reasons for that. George is at his best as a force-multiplier, and he's on a team on which he doesn't need to play an enormous role. Brown is at his best as a floor-raiser, but he's on a team full of floor-raisers. That doesn't mean Philadelphia regrets the trade -- it got them LeBron James! -- but it does suggest that, after months of criticism, the Celtics at least got what they were looking for out of the deal.

Everything the Celtics were good at a year ago, they're still good at. They were one of the NBA's best shooting teams last season, and George both makes more 3s than Brown and takes far more of them. They were great at protecting the basket last season and George's activity as a helper has been a net benefit to their rim-protection.

Yet George's presence has also been the catalyst for improvement in a few other key areas. Boston never generated turnovers defensively last season and they do this year, in part because George is averaging the sixth-most steals and third-most deflections in the NBA. They're getting to the line at a roughly league-average rate, in part because the ball doesn't stick to George as it so often did Brown. It's easier to get defenses in rotation with the ball moving and 3-pointers flying. Tatum has benefited enormously in this respect with a career-best 46% free-throw rate.

Again, the 76ers are perfectly happy with their end of the deal. They traded old for young. They got James on the minimum. They're 11-3. But Boston emerged with the player who has made a bigger difference thus far this season, and it got two first-round draft assets in the process. That doesn't mean the Celtics necessarily win the trade in the long run, but it does suggest, unsurprisingly, that Brad Stevens understood his own team and what it needed better than the rest of us.

Well, they haven't lost in three weeks... so this feels overdue. Let's talk about the much ballyhooed three-guard lineup for a moment. The Spurs couldn't keep bringing Dylan Harper off the bench this season. He's simply too good and too important to their future to risk alienating. They couldn't bench De'Aaron Fox immediately either. Former All-Stars tend to take such decisions as a sign of disrespect, and such a move could have splintered the locker room.

So the Spurs made the somewhat awkward decision to start the three of them together. The season's second game, a loss to the Houston Rockets, showcased exactly why so many feared the fit of the three of them together. Three iffy guard-sized shooters minimized spacing for the sake of redundant ball-handling, and the Harper-Fox-Stephon Castle trio got outscored by 12 points in a four-point defeat. Well, the three guards haven't lost their minutes together in a single game since then. They're +112 in 115 minutes after that point.

Now, there are notable caveats here. Every three-man combination of Spurs that has played at least 100 minutes since then is firmly positive, and the three guards have literally not played a single minute together this season that did not come alongside Victor Wembanyama. It's entirely possible that Wembanyama is so game-breaking that any lineup he's a part of is an almost automatic winner. But that would work in favor of the three guards here. Maybe San Antonio is so much more talented than the field that it can afford to play suboptimal lineups for the sake of maintaining harmony in the locker room.

That may prove more challenging late in a playoff series, but it's easier to convince players to change their roles for, say, Game 5 of the Western Conference Finals than it is in November or December. The Spurs might have to think harder about this in a field that included a healthy Oklahoma City, but with the Thunder compromised, San Antonio is such a large favorite to win the Western Conference that it can afford to try to just out-talent everyone else. So far, it's clearly working.

We are in all-out panic mode over the state of Cleveland's starting lineup. James Harden can't get to the rim anymore. Donovan Mitchell just signed a supermax extension that already feels iffy. Peyton Watson's shooting has fallen off a cliff and he's struggling as a primary point-of-attack defender. The Evan Mobley-Jarrett Allen partnership is getting crushed in its joint minutes. The starters have played 99 minutes together and lost those minutes by 24 points. No five-man unit that has played that many minutes has been outscored by more. Malaise doesn't do this core justice. Clearly, something here has to change.

Fortunately, there appear to be some internal solutions here. After FAA issues forced the Cavaliers to spend Friday night in Miami, Mitchell called for Saturday's game against the Dallas Mavericks to be postponed. The Cavaliers didn't arrive in Dallas until around noon on Saturday. The starters sat out. Cleveland won the game by 10 against a healthy, playoff-caliber opponent. Tyrese Proctor, Meleek Thomas, Mario Hezonja and Jaylon Tyson all scored between 18 and 24 points.

This wasn't a one-off. Thomas is outscoring Harden and Mobley on a per-minute basis. Proctor is sporting a better-than-6-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio on the season, and Synergy Sports rates him in the 100th percentile on spot-up efficiency and the 96th in pick-and-rolls, including passes, in terms of points per possession. Tyson breathes life into a transition offense that is otherwise a sore spot. Most of this team's energy comes from the bench.

What exactly the solution here is, we can't say. It will involve a trade. Perhaps a few. But there's something here, and the early indications are that things are going to get better for the team as a whole when it eventually starts leaning on these players a bit more.

Dejounte Murray requested a trade this week. That's not a rumor. The Pelicans publicly acknowledged it and Murray retweeted the news from ESPN. Meanwhile, after Monday's loss to the Golden State Warriors, Jordan Poole was asked if he would ever come back to the team with which he started his career. He answered "yes." Players tend to not be that definitive in those statements, nor do they tend to acknowledge that their former team "just feels like home." It certainly seems as though there's somewhere he'd rather be than New Orleans.

To borrow a phrase from social media user Nathan Calvin, "if you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two." Essentially... if two players seem this eager to flee, more probably do as well. Sam Amick suggested in a radio interview over the summer that Trey Murphy would like to play elsewhere. There has been plenty of speculation about other Pelicans as well. A 4-10 start following 26- and 21-win seasons tends to do that.

We're more than a year into Joe Dumars' reign as head of basketball operations and there's no discernible plan here. Virtually every key player from last year's roster was retained and the team has largely been healthier than it was a year ago, but they're on pace for a worse record under new head coach Jamahl Mosley. The sad thing is that the Pelicans have a fair number of valuable players. They've just assembled those players so carelessly that they've become far less than the sum of their parts. This team is incoherent, and even the players seem to know it.

Trae Young was held scoreless in 26 minutes on Sunday. It was the first time he's been held scoreless in his entire NBA career, but it may be the final straw of a trend that has been bubbling for some time: Trae Young is simply no longer a star-level scorer. He currently has his lowest shooting percentage from both 2-point and 3-point range in a single season. He lacks the burst to get to the rim or beat mismatches consistently anymore, and he's never developed comfort as a catch-and-shooter. Aside from free throws, it's basically all jumpers off the dribble and floaters, neither of which he's making at the rate he needs to in order to justify his defensive shortcomings. He scored 37 points against Detroit last Monday, but needed 17 free throws to get there on less than 35% shooting from the floor. He needs whistles right now.

This is a version of Young who probably shouldn't monopolize an offense, yet he's never shown that he's capable of playing differently. The Wizards are spending 26 possessions a game on shots Young generates either for himself or a teammate out of pick-and-roll, more than any other player in the league, per Synergy Sports. As of Sunday, he and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander were tied for the league lead among starters in average seconds possessing the ball per touch, per NBA.com tracking data. The younger players who represent the future of this organization are spending a whole lot of time watching someone else dribble. Nobody is really spacing the floor for anyone else since there's so little shooting on this roster. The Wizards have played close to neutral when Young rests, but are getting outscored by more than 10 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor. That difference is almost entirely offensive, yet Young remains the same defensive liability he's always been.

This is where the four-year max contract Washington bewilderingly gave Young becomes so destructive. The basic notion of acquiring a high-end point guard to serve as an offensive organizer for these young wings made sense on paper, but they committed to him essentially sight unseen. He played five mostly meaningless games in a tanking season and they paid him max money without really knowing how he'd fit with the team they were building. If he'd walked for nothing in free agency, well, it's not as though they spent picks to get him. Now they're stuck paying star-level money for a non-star-level player who probably can't meaningfully scale down his involvement in the offense because he just doesn't provide much value when any other player on either team has the basketball.

There are a lot of things going wrong in Washington right now, but Young is inevitably going to be the face of those struggles because he's the player the Wizards just bewilderingly gave a four-year max contract to in order to re-sign. Jaylen Brown had the loudest individual loss of the week, but he at least won all of his other games and has largely been what his team has asked him to be. Young went winless this week, had a scoreless game, and maintained his mostly disappointing season-long performance.

If you would have heard "the Warriors have a -2.4 net rating a month into the 2026-27 season," you probably would have shrugged and said, "sure, sounds about right." The Warriors were widely pegged as a low-end Play-In, high-end lottery team before the season, and a -2.4 net rating projects out to a win total in the 30s. Except that isn't Golden State's net rating. It's Golden State's net rating in the minutes Stephen Curry has missed this season.

That's how far above expectations Golden State was playing during its eight-game winning streak. The Curry-off version of the team was around average; the Curry-on version of the team was a juggernaut. The latter feels a bit unsustainable, but we won't know again for around a month. The former is what's about to be tested now that Curry has an oblique abdominal tear. The Spurs hardly represent a fair test for a team in this situation, but San Antonio predictably waxed Golden State by 38 in the first game of Curry's absence.

Nobody's asking for another eight-game winning streak. Those wins are banked, and Golden State's season begins in earnest when Jimmy Butler returns in January or February. For now, the Warriors just need to stay afloat. Find wins where the schedule offers them, and fortunately, the Pelicans, Kings, Clippers and Jazz are on the docket in the next three weeks or so. But losing Curry is a reminder of how fragile that streak really was. Maybe, now that Yaxel Lendeborg is emerging as a possible star, the Warriors are capable of genuine postseason success this season. But the health of any 38-year-old not named LeBron James is going to be precarious. Things could be a lot worse, but Curry's injury drags one of the feel-good stories of the early season back down to Earth.

#2741. Kane out for 'few months' with ankle ligament tear

England captain Harry Kane will be out "for the next few months" after tearing ligaments in his left ankle during Bayern Munich's 1-1 Bundesliga draw with Cologne on Friday.

The striker, who last month won the Ballon d'Or for the world's best player, was forced off after 20 minutes following a challenge from defender Joel Schmied.

The 33-year-old initially tried to continue before being limping off the pitch to be replaced by Tom Bischof.

A Bayern statement said Kane had "suffered a torn syndesmotic ligament in his left ankle" and would "therefore be sidelined for the next few months".

Bayern trailed to a goal from England Under-21 winger Mikey Moore - who is on loan at Cologne from Tottenham - at the time, before they equalised through a Nathaniel Brown goal in Kompany's first game back after a five-game absence.

Kompany had been absent after being diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

Kane's injury comes on the same day England were drawn against Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals, with the two legs on 27 and 30 March.

He had scored for his country in wins against Croatia and Spain this month to help England finish top of their Nations League group, with this being Bayern's first game back after the international break.

Kane has scored four goals and registered eight assists in 10 league appearances this season, while managing four goals and three assists in four Champions League games.

Kane has had a good fitness record since his move to Germany from Tottenham in August 2023, but he does have a history of ankle issues.

He injured his left ankle playing for Bayern in March 2024, prior to an international break, and missed friendlies against Brazil and Belgium.

While at Spurs, the striker was ruled out for two significant spells in the second half of the 2018-19 season, missing seven games when he damaged ligaments in his left ankle and then nine more matches with a lateral ligament injury.

In 2017-18 he missed a month with a similar injury to the right ankle, and endured separate absences of six and four weeks during the 2016-17 campaign.
